nodes.label: Using scientific models to explain and predict
nodes.objective: Use representational, spatial, descriptive, computational and mathematical models to explain and predict phenomena.
essentialPoints: Models represent real phenomena to aid explanation and prediction
Models can be tested against experimental/observational data
Models have limitations and can be shown to break down

nodes.label: Power and limitations of science, and ethical issues
nodes.objective: Appreciate that science cannot answer all questions and that some questions raise ethical issues.
essentialPoints: Data may be uncertain, incomplete, or unavailable, limiting what science can answer
Some questions involve ethical judgements science alone cannot resolve

nodes.label: Independent, dependent and control variables
nodes.objective: Identify and distinguish independent, dependent and control variables in an investigation.
essentialPoints: Independent variable is changed/selected by the investigator
Dependent variable is measured for each change in the independent variable
Control variables are kept constant so comparisons are fair

nodes.label: Using scientific vocabulary and definitions correctly
nodes.objective: Use correct scientific vocabulary, terminology and definitions in written and spoken explanations.
essentialPoints: Precise scientific terms must be used with their exact accepted meaning
Definitions should be stated using established scientific vocabulary

nodes.label: Recognising and using decimal form
nodes.objective: Recognise and use expressions in decimal form.
essentialPoints: Decimal form expresses quantities using place value with a decimal point

nodes.label: Solving simple algebraic equations
nodes.objective: Solve simple algebraic equations for an unknown quantity.
essentialPoints: Solving an equation isolates the unknown value using valid algebraic steps

nodes.label: Understanding and using mathematical symbols (=, <, >, ∝, ~)
nodes.objective: Understand and correctly use symbols including =, <, <<, >>, >, ∝, ~ in scientific contexts.
essentialPoints: Each symbol has a precise mathematical meaning (e.g. ∝ means 'directly proportional to')
Correct use of these symbols allows concise expression of relationships between quantities

nodes.label: Using angular measures in degrees
nodes.objective: Use angular measures in degrees, including for reflection and refraction contexts.
essentialPoints: Angles are measured in degrees from a specified reference line (e.g. the normal)

nodes.label: Visualising and representing 2D and 3D forms
nodes.objective: Visualise and represent 2D and 3D forms, including 2D representations of 3D objects, e.g. ray diagrams and field patterns.
essentialPoints: 3D physical situations are often represented using 2D diagrams (e.g. cross-sections, ray diagrams)
Interpreting such diagrams requires understanding the spatial relationships they represent

nodes.label: Calculating areas and volumes of simple shapes
nodes.objective: Calculate areas of triangles and rectangles, and surface areas and volumes of cubes, for use in physics calculations.
essentialPoints: Area of a rectangle = length × width; area of a triangle = ½ × base × height
Volume of a cube = side³; surface area of a cube = 6 × side²

nodes.label: Using an appropriate number of significant figures in calculations
nodes.objective: Express calculated and measured quantities to an appropriate number of significant figures
essentialPoints: Significant figures reflect the precision of measurements and calculations
Answers should not imply greater precision than the data allows

nodes.label: Finding arithmetic means from repeat readings
nodes.objective: Calculate the mean of a set of repeated measurements
essentialPoints: Repeating measurements and averaging reduces the effect of random error

nodes.label: Changing the subject of an equation
nodes.objective: Rearrange algebraic equations to solve for a required variable
essentialPoints: An equation can be rearranged to make any variable the subject
This is needed to substitute and solve for unknowns

nodes.label: Substituting numerical values into equations with correct units
nodes.objective: Substitute given quantities and units into a physics equation to calculate a result
essentialPoints: Values must be substituted with consistent SI units
The correct unit must be given with the final answer

nodes.label: Understanding y = mx + c for a linear relationship
nodes.objective: Recognise and interpret a straight-line graph relationship
essentialPoints: A linear graph has a constant gradient (m) and a y-intercept (c)
Gradient and intercept can be linked to physical quantities in an experiment

nodes.label: Plotting two variables from experimental data
nodes.objective: Plot a graph of one measured variable against another from a results table
essentialPoints: Axes must be labelled with quantity and unit
Points should be plotted accurately and a line of best fit drawn

nodes.label: Determining the gradient and intercept of a linear graph
nodes.objective: Calculate the gradient and read the intercept from a straight-line graph
essentialPoints: Gradient = change in y / change in x, using a large triangle
The intercept is where the line crosses the y-axis

nodes.label: Calculating areas of rectangles/triangles and volumes of cubes
nodes.objective: Calculate simple geometric areas and volumes needed for physics calculations
essentialPoints: Area of rectangle = length x width; area of triangle = 0.5 x base x height
Volume of a cube/cuboid = length x width x height

nodes.label: AT1: Using apparatus to measure mass, time and temperature accurately
nodes.objective: Use balances, timers and thermometers correctly to record accurate measurements
essentialPoints: Balances are used to measure mass, timers for time intervals, thermometers for temperature
Readings should be taken at eye level / with correct technique to avoid parallax and zero errors

nodes.label: AT5: Using apparatus safely to measure energy changes/transfers and work done
nodes.objective: Safely set up and use apparatus (e.g. joulemeters, immersion heaters, newton meters) to measure energy transfer and work done
essentialPoints: Energy transfer apparatus must be used with attention to safety (e.g. hot elements, electrical hazards)
Work done can be measured via force and distance moved

nodes.label: A system as an object or group of objects
nodes.objective: Define what is meant by a 'system' in the context of energy transfers
essentialPoints: A system is an object or a group of objects being considered together

nodes.label: Standard circuit diagram symbols
nodes.objective: Recognise and use standard circuit symbols
essentialPoints: Standard symbols exist for common components (cell, battery, switch, lamp, resistor, variable resistor, diode, LED, thermistor, LDR, ammeter, voltmeter, fuse, motor)
Circuit diagrams represent real circuits using these symbols

nodes.label: The National Grid as a system of cables and transformers
nodes.objective: Describe the National Grid as a system linking power stations to consumers
essentialPoints: The National Grid is a system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers
Electrical power is transferred from power stations to consumers using the National Grid

nodes.label: Production of static charge and sparking by rubbing surfaces
nodes.objective: Describe how static electricity is produced and evidenced by sparking when insulating surfaces are rubbed together
essentialPoints: When certain insulating materials are rubbed together they become electrically charged
Sparking can occur due to the build-up of static charge

nodes.label: AT1: using apparatus to measure length, mass, time, volume and temperature accurately
nodes.objective: Use appropriate apparatus (ruler, balance, stopwatch, measuring cylinder, thermometer) to make accurate measurements.
essentialPoints: Select and read appropriate apparatus for length, mass, time, volume, temperature
Take readings avoiding parallax and zero errors
Record measurements with appropriate units and precision

nodes.label: AT1: using a ruler, micrometer or Vernier calliper to measure small dimensions
nodes.objective: Use a micrometer or Vernier calliper to measure small lengths precisely.
essentialPoints: Read a micrometer/Vernier calliper scale correctly including vernier subdivisions
Choose the appropriate instrument based on required precision

nodes.label: AT1: determining volume of an irregular solid by displacement
nodes.objective: Use a displacement technique with a measuring cylinder to find the volume of an irregularly shaped object.
essentialPoints: Submerge object fully in liquid in a measuring cylinder
Volume of object = change in liquid level reading
Read cylinder scale at eye level to avoid parallax

nodes.label: MS2a: using an appropriate number of significant figures
nodes.objective: Round calculated answers to an appropriate number of significant figures.
essentialPoints: Identify significant figures in a given number
Round final answers to match precision of data given

nodes.label: MS2b: finding arithmetic means
nodes.objective: Calculate the mean of a set of repeated measurements.
essentialPoints: Sum values and divide by number of readings
Use mean to reduce effect of random error

nodes.label: MS3b: changing the subject of an equation
nodes.objective: Rearrange an algebraic equation to make a different variable the subject.
essentialPoints: Apply inverse operations to isolate a variable
Rearrange equations with multiplication/division and squares

nodes.label: MS: substituting values into equations with units
nodes.objective: Substitute numerical values with correct units into algebraic equations.
essentialPoints: Insert given quantities with correct SI units into a formula and evaluate

nodes.label: MS4c: plotting two variables from experimental data
nodes.objective: Plot a graph of one variable against another from a table of experimental results.
essentialPoints: Choose sensible scales and axes with labels and units
Plot points accurately and draw a line/curve of best fit

nodes.label: MS4d: determining the gradient and intercept of a linear graph
nodes.objective: Calculate the gradient and y-intercept of a straight-line graph and relate to y = mx + c.
essentialPoints: Gradient = change in y / change in x using a large triangle
Intercept read from where line crosses the y-axis

nodes.label: WS3.7: evaluating accuracy, precision, repeatability, reproducibility and identifying random/systematic error
nodes.objective: Evaluate an experimental method by identifying sources of random and systematic error and suggesting improvements.
essentialPoints: Distinguish accuracy, precision, repeatability and reproducibility
Identify random error (scatter) vs systematic error (consistent offset)
Suggest specific improvements to reduce identified errors

nodes.label: WS2.2: planning experiments with controlled and independent/dependent variables
nodes.objective: Plan an experiment identifying the independent, dependent and control variables.
essentialPoints: Identify the independent variable being changed
Identify the dependent variable being measured
Identify variables that must be controlled/kept constant

nodes.label: Density: definition and equation (ρ = m/V)
nodes.objective: Define density as mass per unit volume and state the equation linking density, mass and volume.
essentialPoints: density = mass / volume, ρ = m/V
Units: kg/m³, mass in kg, volume in m³

nodes.label: Particle model diagrams of solids, liquids and gases
nodes.objective: Recognise and draw simple diagrams representing the arrangement and spacing of particles in solids, liquids and gases.
essentialPoints: Solids: particles closely packed, regular arrangement, vibrate in place
Liquids: particles close together but able to move/slide past each other
Gases: particles far apart, moving randomly at high speed

nodes.label: Work: the transfer of energy by a force
nodes.objective: Define work as the transfer of energy by a force acting on an object.
essentialPoints: Work is energy transferred when a force causes displacement
Work done on a gas transfers energy into it

nodes.label: Basic structure of the atom: nucleus, protons, neutrons, electrons
nodes.objective: Describe the nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons and their charges.
essentialPoints: Nucleus is positively charged, contains protons and neutrons
Electrons are negatively charged and surround the nucleus

nodes.label: Early model: atom as indivisible sphere
nodes.objective: State that before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny indivisible spheres.
essentialPoints: Pre-electron model: atoms are solid, indivisible spheres

nodes.label: AT1: measuring length, mass, time accurately
nodes.objective: Use apparatus to make and record accurate measurements of length, mass and time.
essentialPoints: Use rulers/calipers for length, balances for mass, timers for time
Read to appropriate precision and repeat for reliability

nodes.label: AT2: measuring force and extension of springs
nodes.objective: Use appropriate apparatus to measure force and observe/measure spring extension.
essentialPoints: Attach masses/newtonmeter to spring and measure length changes
Record force applied and resulting extension for a force-extension graph

nodes.label: AT3: measuring motion (speed, acceleration)
nodes.objective: Use appropriate apparatus and techniques to measure speed and rate of change of speed.
essentialPoints: Use light gates, ticker timers or data loggers to record distance/time data
Calculate speed and acceleration from measured data

nodes.label: MS: changing the subject of an equation
nodes.objective: Rearrange equations to make a different variable the subject.
essentialPoints: Manipulate algebraic equations to isolate the required variable

nodes.label: MS: proportionality symbol and direct proportion
nodes.objective: Recognise and use the symbol for proportionality and understand direct proportion between two variables.
essentialPoints: ∝ symbol means 'is directly proportional to'
Doubling one variable doubles the other in direct proportion

nodes.label: MS: plotting graphs and determining gradient/intercept
nodes.objective: Plot two variables from data and determine the gradient and intercept of a linear graph.
essentialPoints: y = mx + c represents a linear relationship
Gradient calculated as change in y over change in x
Intercept read from where line crosses axis

nodes.label: MS: drawing a tangent to a curve
nodes.objective: Draw a tangent to a curved graph at a point to find the gradient there.
essentialPoints: A tangent is a straight line touching a curve at one point without crossing it
Gradient of tangent gives instantaneous rate of change

nodes.label: MS: finding area under a graph (counting squares)
nodes.objective: Determine area under a graph including by counting squares for non-linear regions.
essentialPoints: Area under a graph can represent a physical quantity
Count squares and use scale to estimate area under curved sections

nodes.label: MS: using appropriate significant figures
nodes.objective: Express calculated answers to an appropriate number of significant figures.
essentialPoints: Round final answers to match precision of given data

nodes.label: WS: developing hypotheses and planning investigations
nodes.objective: Use scientific theories to develop hypotheses and plan a valid procedure.
essentialPoints: A hypothesis is a testable prediction based on scientific reasoning
Planning involves identifying variables to control, change and measure

nodes.label: WS: evaluating methods, accuracy, precision and error
nodes.objective: Evaluate experimental methods identifying random and systematic errors and suggest improvements.
essentialPoints: Accuracy vs precision vs repeatability vs reproducibility
Random error causes scatter; systematic error causes a consistent bias
Improvements target the specific source of error identified

nodes.label: Scalar and vector quantities
nodes.objective: Distinguish scalar quantities (magnitude only) from vector quantities (magnitude and direction).
essentialPoints: Scalar quantities have magnitude only (e.g. speed, distance)
Vector quantities have magnitude and direction (e.g. force, velocity)
A vector can be represented by an arrow: length = magnitude, direction = direction

nodes.label: Transverse waves: definition and examples
nodes.objective: Describe transverse waves and give examples such as water ripples and EM waves.
essentialPoints: Oscillations perpendicular to direction of energy transfer
Water ripples are an example of a transverse wave

nodes.label: Longitudinal waves: definition, compression and rarefaction
nodes.objective: Describe longitudinal waves in terms of compressions and rarefactions and give sound as an example.
essentialPoints: Oscillations parallel to direction of energy transfer
Show areas of compression and rarefaction
Sound waves in air are longitudinal

nodes.label: Frequency of a wave
nodes.objective: Define frequency as the number of waves passing a point each second.
essentialPoints: Number of complete waves passing a fixed point per second, measured in Hz

nodes.label: Wave speed: definition
nodes.objective: Define wave speed as the speed at which energy is transferred through a medium.
essentialPoints: Speed at which the wave/energy moves through a medium

nodes.label: Poles of a magnet: attraction and repulsion between like/unlike poles
nodes.objective: Describe attraction and repulsion between like and unlike magnetic poles.
essentialPoints: The poles of a magnet are where magnetic force is strongest
Two like poles repel; two unlike poles attract
Attraction/repulsion between magnetic poles is a non-contact force

nodes.label: Structure of the solar system: Sun, planets, dwarf planets, natural satellites
nodes.objective: State the components of the solar system and their arrangement.
essentialPoints: One star (the Sun) with eight planets and dwarf planets orbiting it
Natural satellites (moons) orbit planets
Solar system is part of the Milky Way galaxy

nodes.label: Distinction between speed (scalar) and velocity (vector)
nodes.objective: Distinguish velocity (speed with direction) from speed (magnitude only), as required to understand circular motion.
essentialPoints: Speed is a scalar quantity (magnitude only)
Velocity is a vector quantity (magnitude and direction)
An object can change velocity while speed stays constant if direction changes

nodes.label: Definition of wavelength
nodes.objective: Recall wavelength as the distance between corresponding points on successive waves.
essentialPoints: Wavelength is the distance between two corresponding points on adjacent waves (e.g. crest to crest)

nodes.label: The Big Bang theory: universe began from a small, hot, dense region
nodes.objective: State the Big Bang theory of the origin of the universe.
essentialPoints: The Big Bang theory proposes the universe began from a very small region
This region was extremely hot and dense
The universe has been expanding ever since

nodes.label: Scientific methods and theories develop over time with new evidence
nodes.objective: Understand that scientific models/theories change as new data emerges.
essentialPoints: Theories are provisional and change when new data emerges
New observations/experiments can support or refute existing models

nodes.label: Technological applications of science and their implications
nodes.objective: Explain everyday/technological applications of science and evaluate personal, social, economic and environmental implications.
essentialPoints: Scientific applications have personal, social, economic and environmental consequences
Evaluating an application means weighing these implications using evidence

nodes.label: Developing a hypothesis from theory
nodes.objective: Use scientific theories and explanations to develop a testable hypothesis.
essentialPoints: A hypothesis is a testable proposed explanation derived from existing theory
Hypotheses must be capable of being supported or refuted by evidence

nodes.label: Scientific quantities and how they are determined
nodes.objective: Recognise the importance of scientific quantities and understand how they are measured or determined.
essentialPoints: A physical quantity consists of a numerical value and a unit
Quantities are determined by defined measurement procedures using appropriate instruments

nodes.label: Using ratios, fractions and percentages
nodes.objective: Use ratios, fractions and percentages to solve numerical problems in physics contexts.
essentialPoints: A ratio compares two or more quantities of the same kind
Percentages and fractions are used to express proportions of a whole, including efficiency-style calculations

nodes.label: Changing the subject of an equation
nodes.objective: Rearrange an algebraic equation to make a different quantity the subject.
essentialPoints: Rearranging isolates the required unknown on one side of the equation
The same operation must be applied to both sides to preserve equality

nodes.label: Efficiency equation using useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer
nodes.objective: Recall and apply the equation for efficiency in terms of energy transfers
essentialPoints: efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer
Efficiency can be expressed as a decimal or percentage

nodes.label: Energy stores (kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, magnetic, electrostatic, nuclear)
nodes.objective: Identify the ways energy can be stored in a system
essentialPoints: Energy can be stored in named ways: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal (internal), chemical, magnetic, electrostatic, nuclear

nodes.label: Drawing and interpreting circuit diagrams
nodes.objective: Draw and interpret circuit diagrams using standard symbols
essentialPoints: Circuit diagrams can be drawn and read using standard symbols
A given diagram shows how components are connected (series/parallel arrangement)

nodes.label: Step-up and step-down transformers in the National Grid
nodes.objective: Describe the role of step-up and step-down transformers in the National Grid
essentialPoints: Step-up transformers increase the pd from the power station to the transmission cables
Step-down transformers decrease the pd to a much lower value for domestic use

nodes.label: Electron transfer explains static charging
nodes.objective: Explain how the transfer of electrons between objects produces static electricity
essentialPoints: Negatively charged electrons are rubbed off one material onto the other
The material gaining electrons becomes negatively charged; the material losing electrons is left with an equal positive charge

nodes.label: RP5 procedure: measuring mass and volume of a liquid sample
nodes.objective: Measure the mass and volume of a liquid sample using a balance and measuring cylinder.
essentialPoints: Measure mass of empty and filled container to find liquid mass
Read liquid volume directly from a measuring cylinder

nodes.label: RP5 procedure: measuring dimensions of a regular solid to find volume
nodes.objective: Measure the dimensions of a regularly shaped solid using a ruler, micrometer or Vernier calliper and calculate its volume.
essentialPoints: Measure length, width, height (or diameter) using appropriate apparatus
Calculate volume using the relevant geometric formula

nodes.label: RP5 procedure: finding volume of an irregular solid by displacement
nodes.objective: Use the displacement technique to determine the volume of an irregularly shaped solid.
essentialPoints: Lower object into a measuring cylinder of liquid
Record rise in liquid level as the object's volume

nodes.label: Calculating density, mass or volume using ρ = m/V
nodes.objective: Apply and rearrange the density equation to find density, mass or volume, including where mass is conserved.
essentialPoints: Rearrange ρ = m/V to find m or V
Apply equation to changes where mass is conserved

nodes.label: Explaining density differences between states using the particle model
nodes.objective: Explain why solids, liquids and gases typically have different densities in terms of particle arrangement and spacing.
essentialPoints: Closer particle packing gives higher density (more mass per volume)
Gases have low density because particles are widely spaced
Explains why solids/liquids are usually denser than gases

nodes.label: Changes of state: mass is conserved
nodes.objective: Describe that when a substance changes state (melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing, subliming), its total mass is conserved.
essentialPoints: Named changes of state: melt, freeze, boil, evaporate, condense, sublimate
Total mass before and after a change of state is unchanged

nodes.label: Internal energy: total kinetic and potential energy of particles in a system
nodes.objective: Define internal energy as the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all particles that make up a system.
essentialPoints: Internal energy = sum of kinetic energy (particle motion) and potential energy (particle bonds/positions)
Energy is stored within a system by its particles

nodes.label: Molecules in a gas are in constant random motion
nodes.objective: Describe that gas molecules move constantly and randomly in all directions.
essentialPoints: Gas molecules move continuously and randomly
Molecules travel in straight lines between collisions

nodes.label: Atomic radius (~1×10⁻¹⁰ m) and nuclear radius (<1/10000 of atom)
nodes.objective: State the approximate size of an atom and its nucleus relative to each other.
essentialPoints: Atom radius ~1×10⁻¹⁰ m
Nucleus radius <1/10000 of atom radius
Most mass concentrated in nucleus

nodes.label: Electron energy levels and radiation absorption/emission
nodes.objective: Explain how electrons occupy discrete energy levels and how absorption/emission of EM radiation changes their level.
essentialPoints: Electrons arranged at different distances (energy levels) from nucleus
Absorbing EM radiation moves an electron to a higher energy level (further from nucleus)
Emitting EM radiation moves an electron to a lower energy level (closer to nucleus)

nodes.label: Atoms have no overall charge (protons = electrons)
nodes.objective: State that the number of electrons equals the number of protons in a neutral atom.
essentialPoints: Number of electrons = number of protons in an atom
This gives the atom no overall electrical charge

nodes.label: Plum pudding model
nodes.objective: Describe the plum pudding model following the discovery of the electron.
essentialPoints: Atom is a ball of positive charge
Negative electrons are embedded within the positive charge

nodes.label: Contact and non-contact forces
nodes.objective: Define force and classify examples as contact or non-contact forces.
essentialPoints: A force is a push or pull from an interaction between two objects
Contact forces require physical touching: friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact force
Non-contact forces act at a distance: gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic force

nodes.label: Distance and displacement
nodes.objective: Distinguish distance (scalar) from displacement (vector, with magnitude and direction).
essentialPoints: Distance is how far an object moves, with no direction (scalar)
Displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish plus direction (vector)

nodes.label: Speed as a scalar quantity
nodes.objective: Understand speed as a scalar quantity that is rarely constant in everyday motion.
essentialPoints: Speed has magnitude only, no direction (scalar)
Real-world speeds (walking, running, driving) are rarely constant

nodes.label: Amplitude of a wave
nodes.objective: Define amplitude as the maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its undisturbed position.
essentialPoints: Maximum displacement from the undisturbed (rest) position

nodes.label: S-waves: properties (Physics only, HT only)
nodes.objective: Describe S-waves as transverse seismic waves that cannot travel through a liquid.
essentialPoints: S-waves are transverse seismic waves
S-waves cannot travel through a liquid

nodes.label: Electromagnetic waves: definition as transverse waves carrying energy
nodes.objective: Define electromagnetic waves as transverse waves that transfer energy from a source to an absorber.
essentialPoints: EM waves are transverse waves
They transfer energy from a source to an absorber

nodes.label: Evidence that it is the wave, not the medium, that travels
nodes.objective: Describe evidence that for water ripples and sound waves it is the wave, not the water or air, that travels.
essentialPoints: A floating object on water bobs up and down but does not travel with the ripple
Air particles oscillate about a fixed position rather than moving with the sound wave

nodes.label: Wavelength of a wave
nodes.objective: Define wavelength as the distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave.
essentialPoints: Distance between equivalent points on adjacent waves

nodes.label: Sound-to-vibration conversion processes, including the ear (Physics only, HT only)
nodes.objective: Describe examples of processes converting wave disturbances between sound waves and vibrations in solids, including the ear drum.
essentialPoints: Sound waves travelling through solids cause vibrations in the solid
Within the ear, sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate, producing the sensation of sound

nodes.label: P-waves: properties (Physics only, HT only)
nodes.objective: Describe P-waves as longitudinal seismic waves that travel at different speeds through solids and liquids.
essentialPoints: P-waves are longitudinal seismic waves
P-waves travel through both solids and liquids at different speeds in each

nodes.label: Period-frequency equation: T = 1/f
nodes.objective: Recall and apply period = 1/frequency.
essentialPoints: T = 1/f
Period in seconds, frequency in hertz

nodes.label: Reflection, transmission and absorption of waves at a boundary (Physics only)
nodes.objective: Describe that waves can be reflected, transmitted or absorbed at the boundary between two materials.
essentialPoints: Waves can be reflected at a boundary between two different materials
Waves can instead be absorbed or transmitted at that boundary

nodes.label: Permanent vs induced magnets
nodes.objective: Distinguish permanent magnets from induced magnets.
essentialPoints: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field
An induced magnet becomes magnetic only when placed in a magnetic field
Induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction
An induced magnet loses most/all magnetism quickly when removed from the field

nodes.label: Formation of the Sun from a nebula by gravitational attraction
nodes.objective: Explain that the Sun formed from a cloud of dust and gas pulled together by gravity.
essentialPoints: A nebula is a cloud of dust and gas
Gravitational attraction pulls the nebula together to form a star

nodes.label: Gravity as the force maintaining circular orbits of planets and satellites
nodes.objective: State that gravitational force provides the centripetal force keeping planets and satellites in circular orbits.
essentialPoints: Gravity acts as a centripetal force pulling the orbiting body toward the central mass
This force allows planets, natural satellites and artificial satellites to maintain roughly circular orbits

nodes.label: Red-shift: observed increase in wavelength of light from receding galaxies
nodes.objective: Describe red-shift as the observed increase in wavelength of light from distant galaxies moving away from us.
essentialPoints: Light from most distant galaxies shows an increased wavelength (shifted toward red end of spectrum)
This is called red-shift

nodes.label: Peer review and communicating scientific results
nodes.objective: Recognise the role of peer review in validating scientific claims and communicating findings.
essentialPoints: Peer review checks results before publication to detect false claims and build consensus
Media reports of science are not peer reviewed and may be biased, oversimplified or inaccurate

nodes.label: Evaluating risk in practical science and society
nodes.objective: Evaluate risks in practical science and in wider society, including differences between measured and perceived risk.
essentialPoints: Hazards from science-based technology must be weighed against benefits
Perceived risk can differ from measured risk (e.g. voluntary vs imposed, familiar vs unfamiliar, visible vs invisible)

nodes.label: Planning experiments and procedures
nodes.objective: Devise and justify a procedure to test a hypothesis, manipulating and controlling variables appropriately.
essentialPoints: A well-designed procedure controls variables and directly tests the hypothesis
Explaining why a procedure is well designed requires reference to variable control

nodes.label: Using SI units correctly
nodes.objective: Use SI units (e.g. kg, m, J) appropriately for physical quantities.
essentialPoints: Each physical quantity has a standard SI unit (e.g. kilogram for mass, metre for length, joule for energy)
Consistent use of SI units allows valid calculation and comparison

nodes.label: Kinetic energy equation: Ek = 0.5 x m x v^2
nodes.objective: Recall and apply the equation for kinetic energy of a moving object
essentialPoints: kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x speed^2
Units: energy in joules, mass in kg, speed in m/s

nodes.label: Elastic potential energy equation: Ee = 0.5 x k x e^2
nodes.objective: Recall and apply the equation for elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring, assuming the limit of proportionality is not exceeded
essentialPoints: elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x extension^2
Only valid while the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded
Units: energy in J, spring constant in N/m, extension in m

nodes.label: Gravitational potential energy equation: Ep = m x g x h
nodes.objective: Recall and apply the equation for gravitational potential energy gained by a raised object
essentialPoints: g.p.e. = mass x gravitational field strength x height
g is given in any calculation requiring it
Units: energy in J, mass in kg, g in N/kg, height in m

nodes.label: Definition of power as rate of energy transfer/rate of work done
nodes.objective: Define power as the rate at which energy is transferred or work is done
essentialPoints: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred or the rate at which work is done
1 joule per second = 1 watt

nodes.label: Conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed
nodes.objective: State the principle of conservation of energy
essentialPoints: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored, or dissipated, but the total amount of energy cannot be created or destroyed

nodes.label: Main energy resources available on Earth (fossil fuels, nuclear, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, tides, Sun, water waves)
nodes.objective: Describe the main energy resources available for use on Earth
essentialPoints: Fossil fuels: coal, oil and gas
Nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, tides, the Sun, and water waves are also energy resources

nodes.label: Energy store changes for a projectile (kinetic to gravitational potential)
nodes.objective: Describe the energy store changes when an object is projected upwards.
essentialPoints: An object projected upwards: kinetic store transfers to gravitational potential store

nodes.label: Energy store changes in a collision (kinetic to thermal/sound)
nodes.objective: Describe the energy store changes when a moving object hits an obstacle.
essentialPoints: A moving object hitting an obstacle: kinetic store transfers to thermal/sound stores

nodes.label: Energy store changes for an object accelerated by a constant force
nodes.objective: Describe the energy store changes when an object is accelerated by a constant force.
essentialPoints: An object accelerated by a constant force: work done increases kinetic store

nodes.label: Energy store changes when heating water (e.g. in a kettle)
nodes.objective: Describe the energy store changes when water is heated by an electrical device.
essentialPoints: Heating water in a kettle: chemical/electrical transfer increases thermal store of water

nodes.label: Energy store changes for a decelerating vehicle (kinetic to thermal)
nodes.objective: Describe the energy store changes when a vehicle slows down using brakes.
essentialPoints: A vehicle slowing down: kinetic store transfers to thermal store (brakes)

nodes.label: Closed circuit requires a source of potential difference
nodes.objective: State that a source of pd is needed for charge to flow round a closed circuit
essentialPoints: For electrical charge to flow through a closed circuit, the circuit must include a source of potential difference
Without a pd source, no current flows

nodes.label: Evidence of attraction and repulsion between charged objects
nodes.objective: Describe evidence that charged objects exert forces on each other without contact
essentialPoints: Two objects with the same type of charge repel each other
Two objects with different types of charge attract each other
Attraction and repulsion between charged objects are examples of non-contact force

nodes.label: RP5 evaluation: sources of error in density measurements
nodes.objective: Evaluate sources of error in measuring mass and volume when determining density, and suggest improvements.
essentialPoints: Parallax error reading measuring cylinder scale affects volume for displacement method
Measurement precision of micrometer/Vernier vs ruler affects regular solid volume accuracy
Air bubbles or partially submerged objects cause displacement errors

nodes.label: RP5 application: calculating densities of solids and liquids from measured mass and volume
nodes.objective: Use measured mass and volume data to calculate the density of regular solids, irregular solids and liquids.
essentialPoints: Apply ρ = m/V to collected data for each object/liquid
Compare calculated density to known material values to identify substances

nodes.label: Changes of state are physical changes, reversible with recovery of original properties
nodes.objective: Explain that changes of state are physical changes, distinct from chemical changes, because the material recovers its original properties on reversal.
essentialPoints: Physical change: no new substance formed
Original substance's properties are recovered if the change is reversed

nodes.label: Heating a system: raising temperature or changing state
nodes.objective: Explain that heating changes the internal energy of a system, which either raises its temperature or produces a change of state.
essentialPoints: Heating increases the energy of particles in a system
This increase either raises temperature or causes a change of state, not both at once

nodes.label: Temperature of a gas relates to the average kinetic energy of its molecules
nodes.objective: Explain that the temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules.
essentialPoints: Higher temperature means higher average molecular kinetic energy
This links macroscopic temperature to microscopic particle motion

nodes.label: Explaining gas pressure in terms of particle collisions with container walls
nodes.objective: Explain gas pressure as the result of gas molecules colliding with the walls of their container, producing a net force at right angles to the surface.
essentialPoints: Pressure results from many molecular collisions with container walls
The collisions produce a net force acting at right angles to the wall/surface

nodes.label: Atomic number
nodes.objective: Define atomic number as the number of protons in an atom.
essentialPoints: Atomic number = number of protons in the nucleus
All atoms of a given element have the same atomic number

nodes.label: Ion formation by electron loss/gain
nodes.objective: Explain that atoms become positive ions by losing outer electrons.
essentialPoints: Losing one or more outer electrons produces a positive ion
This disrupts the balance between protons and electrons, giving overall charge

nodes.label: Alpha particle scattering experiment and its conclusions
nodes.objective: Explain how the results of the alpha scattering experiment led to the nuclear model, replacing the plum pudding model.
essentialPoints: Some alpha particles were deflected/bounced back by the atom
This showed most mass and all positive charge is concentrated in a small central nucleus
New evidence caused the scientific model to change (plum pudding replaced by nuclear model)

nodes.label: Interaction pairs of forces as vectors
nodes.objective: Describe the interaction between pairs of objects producing a force on each, represented as vectors.
essentialPoints: Two interacting objects each experience a force from the interaction
Both forces can be represented as vectors (magnitude and direction)

nodes.label: Weight as a force due to gravity
nodes.objective: Define weight as the force on an object due to a gravitational field, distinct from mass.
essentialPoints: Weight is the force acting on an object due to gravity
Gravity near Earth arises from the Earth's gravitational field
Weight depends on the gravitational field strength at that location

nodes.label: Resultant force (forces in a straight line)
nodes.objective: Calculate the resultant of two or more forces acting in a straight line.
essentialPoints: Several forces acting on an object can be replaced by one resultant force with the same effect
Add forces in the same direction, subtract forces in opposite directions

nodes.label: Forces involved in stretching, bending, compressing
nodes.objective: Give examples of forces involved in stretching, bending or compressing an object.
essentialPoints: Stretching, bending and compressing all involve forces applied to an object

nodes.label: Fluids and pressure acting normal to a surface
nodes.objective: Know that a fluid is a liquid or gas and that pressure in fluids acts normal (at right angles) to any surface.
essentialPoints: A fluid is either a liquid or a gas
Pressure in a fluid produces a force perpendicular (normal) to any surface it acts on

nodes.label: Typical speed values for people and transport
nodes.objective: Recall typical values of speed for walking, running, cycling, sound in air, and transport systems.
essentialPoints: Walking ≈ 1.5 m/s, running ≈ 3 m/s, cycling ≈ 6 m/s
Speed of sound in air ≈ 330 m/s
Speed of wind and transport systems also vary

nodes.label: Distance-speed-time equation: s = vt
nodes.objective: Recall and apply distance travelled = speed × time for constant speed, and calculate average speed for non-uniform motion.
essentialPoints: distance (m) = speed (m/s) × time (s), for constant speed
Average speed for non-uniform motion = total distance / total time

nodes.label: Velocity as speed in a given direction
nodes.objective: Define velocity as speed in a given direction, a vector quantity, and apply the vector-scalar distinction consistently.
essentialPoints: Velocity is speed in a given direction (vector)
Applies the scalar/vector distinction across distance, displacement, speed, velocity

nodes.label: EM spectrum is continuous and travels at constant velocity in vacuum/air
nodes.objective: State that the EM spectrum is continuous and all EM waves travel at the same velocity through a vacuum or air.
essentialPoints: EM waves form a continuous spectrum
All types travel at the same speed through a vacuum or air

nodes.label: Examples illustrating energy transfer by EM waves
nodes.objective: Give examples that illustrate the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves.
essentialPoints: E.g. infrared heating an object, or microwaves heating food, demonstrate energy transfer by EM waves

nodes.label: Wave equation: v = fλ
nodes.objective: Recall and apply the wave equation v = fλ.
essentialPoints: wave speed = frequency × wavelength
v in m/s, f in Hz, λ in m

nodes.label: Identify amplitude and wavelength from a wave diagram
nodes.objective: Read off amplitude and wavelength values from a given wave diagram.
essentialPoints: Locate maximum displacement on diagram as amplitude
Locate distance between equivalent points as wavelength

nodes.label: Limited frequency range of hearing and human hearing limits (Physics only, HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain why sound-to-vibration conversion only works over a limited frequency range and state the range of normal human hearing.
essentialPoints: Conversion of sound to vibrations in solids only works efficiently over a limited frequency range
This restricts human hearing to a range from 20 Hz to 20 kHz

nodes.label: Ray diagrams for reflection of a wave at a surface (Physics only)
nodes.objective: Construct ray diagrams to illustrate reflection of a wave at a surface, using angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
essentialPoints: Draw incident ray, normal and reflected ray
Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection

nodes.label: Effects of reflection, transmission and absorption at material interfaces (Physics only)
nodes.objective: Describe the effects of reflection, transmission and absorption of waves at material interfaces.
essentialPoints: Reflected wave changes direction, energy returns to original medium
Transmitted wave continues into second medium, often with a change in direction (refraction) and speed
Absorbed wave's energy is transferred into the material, often as internal/thermal energy

nodes.label: Seismic wave evidence for Earth's structure and core (Physics only, HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain how P-wave and S-wave behaviour provides evidence for the structure and size of the Earth's core.
essentialPoints: S-waves disappearing beyond a certain point shows the outer core is liquid
Changes in P-wave speed and direction give evidence of the size/structure of the core
Study of seismic waves revealed previously unobservable structure of the Earth

nodes.label: Magnetic field: definition and magnetic materials
nodes.objective: Define a magnetic field and identify magnetic materials.
essentialPoints: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or magnetic material
Magnetic materials include iron, steel, cobalt and nickel
The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always attractive

nodes.label: Gravitational collapse triggering fusion at a star's formation
nodes.objective: Explain how gravitational collapse of the nebula causes conditions for fusion reactions to begin.
essentialPoints: Gravity draws dust/gas together, increasing density and temperature at the core
When core temperature/pressure is high enough, fusion reactions begin

nodes.label: Similarities and distinctions between planets, moons and artificial satellites
nodes.objective: Describe similarities and differences between planets, their natural satellites (moons), and artificial satellites.
essentialPoints: All orbit a larger body under gravity
Planets orbit stars, moons orbit planets, artificial satellites are human-made objects placed in orbit (often around Earth)
Artificial satellites differ in origin/purpose (e.g. communications, monitoring) from natural bodies

nodes.label: HT: Circular orbits involve constantly changing velocity but constant speed
nodes.objective: Explain qualitatively how gravity changes the direction (and hence velocity) of an orbiting body while its speed stays constant.
essentialPoints: Gravity acts perpendicular to the direction of travel, continuously changing direction
Because direction changes but magnitude of speed does not, velocity changes even though speed is constant

nodes.label: Relationship between galaxy distance and speed/size of red-shift
nodes.objective: State that more distant galaxies show greater red-shift and are moving away faster.
essentialPoints: The further away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away
The further away a galaxy is, the greater the observed increase in wavelength (bigger red-shift)

nodes.label: Explaining red-shift qualitatively as evidence galaxies are receding
nodes.objective: Explain qualitatively why red-shift indicates galaxies are moving away from us.
essentialPoints: Increase in observed wavelength is caused by the source (galaxy) moving away from the observer
This Doppler-type effect stretches the light's wavelength toward the red end of the spectrum

nodes.label: Selecting appropriate apparatus, techniques and materials
nodes.objective: Apply knowledge of apparatus, techniques and materials to select those appropriate for a given experimental purpose.
essentialPoints: Choice of instrument/apparatus depends on the range and precision needed
Justification requires linking apparatus properties to the purpose of measurement

nodes.label: Sampling techniques for representative data
nodes.objective: Recognise when and how to apply sampling techniques to ensure collected data is representative.
essentialPoints: Sampling is needed when it is impractical to measure an entire population/data set
A representative sample avoids bias in the conclusions drawn

nodes.label: Substituting values into equations with correct units
nodes.objective: Substitute numerical values into algebraic equations using appropriate units for physical quantities.
essentialPoints: Each value substituted must be in units consistent with the equation (e.g. SI base units)
The final answer's unit follows from the units of the substituted quantities

nodes.label: Using prefixes and powers of ten for orders of magnitude
nodes.objective: Use standard prefixes (tera, giga, mega, kilo, centi, milli, micro, nano) to express quantities across orders of magnitude.
essentialPoints: Each prefix corresponds to a specific power of ten multiplier (e.g. kilo = 10^3, milli = 10^-3)
Prefixes allow convenient expression of very large or very small quantities

nodes.label: RP1(AT1 context)/AT1: Investigating the transfer of energy from a gravitational potential energy store to a kinetic energy store
nodes.objective: Carry out an investigation measuring the transfer of gravitational potential energy to kinetic energy as an object falls or rolls down a slope
essentialPoints: Measure height dropped and resulting speed to compare GPE lost and KE gained
Uses length/height and motion measurement apparatus

nodes.label: Power equation: P = E / t
nodes.objective: Recall and apply the equation power = energy transferred / time
essentialPoints: power = energy transferred / time
Units: P in watts, E in joules, t in seconds

nodes.label: Power equation: P = W / t
nodes.objective: Recall and apply the equation power = work done / time
essentialPoints: power = work done / time
Units: P in watts, W in joules, t in seconds

nodes.label: Efficiency equation using useful power output / total power input
nodes.objective: Recall and apply the equation for efficiency in terms of power
essentialPoints: efficiency = useful power output / total power input
Efficiency can be expressed as a decimal or percentage

nodes.label: Closed systems: no net change in total energy
nodes.objective: Describe, with examples, that in a closed system there is no net change to the total energy
essentialPoints: A closed system is one where no energy transfers occur into or out of it
In a closed system total energy before and after any change is the same

nodes.label: Definition of a renewable energy resource
nodes.objective: Define a renewable energy resource as one that is being, or can be, replenished as it is used
essentialPoints: A renewable energy resource is one that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used

nodes.label: Uses of energy resources: transport, electricity generation and heating
nodes.objective: Compare how different energy resources are used for transport, electricity generation and heating
essentialPoints: Energy resources are used for transport (e.g. fossil fuels in vehicles)
Energy resources are used for electricity generation (e.g. wind, fossil fuels, nuclear)
Energy resources are used for heating (e.g. gas, bio-fuel, geothermal, electric heating)

nodes.label: Dissipation of energy to less useful stores ('wasted' energy)
nodes.objective: Describe, with examples, how energy is dissipated in all system changes so that it is stored in less useful ways
essentialPoints: In all system changes, some energy is dissipated (often to a thermal store of the surroundings)
This dissipated energy is often described as 'wasted' because it is less useful

nodes.label: Electric current as rate of flow of charge
nodes.objective: Define electric current as the rate of flow of electrical charge
essentialPoints: Electric current is a flow of electrical charge
The size of the current is the rate of flow of charge

nodes.label: Concept of an electric field around a charged object
nodes.objective: Explain the concept of an electric field around a charged object
essentialPoints: A charged object creates an electric field around itself
The electric field is strongest close to the charged object and weaker further away

nodes.label: Specific heat capacity: definition
nodes.objective: Define specific heat capacity as the energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius.
essentialPoints: Specific heat capacity is energy needed per kg per °C rise
Different materials have different specific heat capacities

nodes.label: Latent heat: energy for a change of state without temperature change
nodes.objective: Explain that energy supplied during a change of state changes the internal energy stored (via potential energy) but not the temperature.
essentialPoints: Latent heat is energy needed for a substance to change state
During a change of state, temperature stays constant while internal energy changes

nodes.label: Effect of changing temperature on pressure of a gas at constant volume
nodes.objective: Explain qualitatively that increasing the temperature of a gas held at constant volume increases its pressure.
essentialPoints: Increasing temperature increases average molecular kinetic energy and collision frequency/force
This increases the pressure exerted by the gas at constant volume

nodes.label: Gases can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes
nodes.objective: State that a gas can be compressed or expanded by changes in pressure.
essentialPoints: A gas's volume can decrease (compression) or increase (expansion) when pressure changes

nodes.label: Mass number
nodes.objective: Define mass number as the total number of protons and neutrons in an atom.
essentialPoints: Mass number = protons + neutrons in the nucleus

nodes.label: Bohr's nuclear model with electron orbits
nodes.objective: Describe Bohr's adaptation of the nuclear model, with electrons orbiting at specific distances, matching experimental observations.
essentialPoints: Bohr suggested electrons orbit the nucleus at fixed, specific distances
Bohr's theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations

nodes.label: Discovery of the proton
nodes.objective: State that the positive charge of the nucleus was found to be subdivided into protons, each with equal positive charge.
essentialPoints: Nuclear positive charge is made of whole-number units, each called a proton
Each proton carries the same amount of positive charge

nodes.label: Weight equation: W = mg
nodes.objective: Recall and apply W = m × g to calculate weight.
essentialPoints: weight (N) = mass (kg) × gravitational field strength (N/kg)
g is given in any calculation

nodes.label: Centre of mass
nodes.objective: Understand that an object's weight may be considered to act at a single point, its centre of mass.
essentialPoints: Centre of mass is the single point where an object's weight can be considered to act

nodes.label: Free body diagrams and balanced forces (HT)
nodes.objective: Use free body diagrams to describe forces on an isolated object, including balanced forces giving zero resultant.
essentialPoints: A free body diagram shows all forces acting on an isolated object/system as arrows
Balanced forces produce a resultant force of zero

nodes.label: Work done by a force causing displacement
nodes.objective: Understand that work is done on an object when a force causes it to move through a distance.
essentialPoints: Work is done when a force causes a displacement of an object
Doing work transfers energy

nodes.label: Forces causing rotation
nodes.objective: Describe examples in which forces cause objects to rotate.
essentialPoints: A force or system of forces can cause an object to rotate about a pivot

nodes.label: Newton's Third Law
nodes.objective: State Newton's Third Law and apply it to equilibrium situations.
essentialPoints: Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite
Apply this to examples of equilibrium (e.g. object resting on a surface)

nodes.label: Why more than one force is needed to change shape of a stationary object
nodes.objective: Explain why changing the shape of a stationary object requires more than one force.
essentialPoints: A stationary object needs balanced forces overall to remain stationary while deforming
A single unbalanced force would simply accelerate the object rather than deform it

nodes.label: Elastic vs inelastic deformation
nodes.objective: Describe the difference between elastic and inelastic deformation caused by stretching forces.
essentialPoints: Elastic deformation: object returns to its original shape/length when the force is removed
Inelastic deformation: object does not return to its original shape/length

nodes.label: Pressure equation: p = F/A
nodes.objective: Recall and apply pressure = force normal to a surface / area of that surface.
essentialPoints: pressure (Pa) = force normal to surface (N) / area of surface (m²)

nodes.label: Simple model of the Earth's atmosphere
nodes.objective: Describe a simple model of the Earth's atmosphere as a thin layer of air that becomes less dense with altitude.
essentialPoints: The atmosphere is a thin layer of air surrounding the Earth relative to Earth's size
Atmospheric density decreases with increasing altitude

nodes.label: Distance-time graphs and gradient as speed
nodes.objective: Draw distance-time graphs from measurements and determine speed from the gradient.
essentialPoints: Distance travelled along a straight line can be plotted as a distance-time graph
The gradient of a distance-time graph gives the speed

nodes.label: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance
nodes.objective: Define stopping distance as the sum of thinking distance and braking distance, increasing with speed.
essentialPoints: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance
For a given braking force, greater speed means greater stopping distance

nodes.label: Circular motion: constant speed, changing velocity (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain qualitatively that motion in a circle involves constant speed but continuously changing velocity due to changing direction.
essentialPoints: An object moving in a circle at constant speed has continuously changing direction
Since velocity is a vector, changing direction means velocity is always changing even if speed is constant

nodes.label: Acceleration equation: a = Δv/t
nodes.objective: Recall and apply average acceleration = change in velocity / time taken, and identify deceleration.
essentialPoints: acceleration (m/s²) = change in velocity (m/s) / time taken (s)
An object that slows down is decelerating (negative acceleration)

nodes.label: Newton's First Law
nodes.objective: State and apply Newton's First Law: an object's velocity only changes if a resultant force acts on it.
essentialPoints: If resultant force is zero and object is stationary, it stays stationary
If resultant force is zero and object is moving, it continues at the same velocity
Velocity only changes if a resultant force acts (e.g. steady speed means driving force balances resistive forces)

nodes.label: Momentum equation: p = mv (HT)
nodes.objective: Recall and apply momentum = mass × velocity.
essentialPoints: momentum (kg m/s) = mass (kg) × velocity (m/s)

nodes.label: Groups of the EM spectrum in order of wavelength/frequency
nodes.objective: State the order of EM spectrum groups from long to short wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray.
essentialPoints: Order (long to short wavelength): radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
Visible light itself ranges from red to violet

nodes.label: Radio waves produced by oscillations in electrical circuits (HT only)
nodes.objective: State that radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits.
essentialPoints: Oscillating currents in a circuit generate radio waves of the same frequency

nodes.label: Radiation dose as a measure of risk of harm
nodes.objective: Describe radiation dose (measured in sieverts) as a measure of the risk of harm from radiation exposure.
essentialPoints: Radiation dose measures risk of harm from exposure to radiation
Measured in sieverts (Sv); 1000 mSv = 1 Sv (unit not required to be recalled)

nodes.label: All bodies emit and absorb infrared radiation; hotter bodies radiate more
nodes.objective: State that all objects emit and absorb infrared radiation, and hotter objects radiate more infrared in a given time.
essentialPoints: All bodies, regardless of temperature, both emit and absorb infrared radiation
The hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time

nodes.label: RP8 procedure: measuring wave properties in a ripple tank and a solid
nodes.objective: Carry out a method to identify suitable apparatus and take measurements of frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in a ripple tank and in a solid.
essentialPoints: Select suitable apparatus (strobe/lamp, ruler, stopwatch, signal generator) to observe waves
Measure wavelength directly from ripple pattern or wave on a solid (e.g. stretched string/spring)
Measure or count frequency of oscillations over a timed period
Calculate speed using measured frequency and wavelength or by timing wave travel over a known distance

nodes.label: Method to measure the speed of sound in air
nodes.objective: Describe a method to measure the speed of sound waves in air.
essentialPoints: Measure time for sound to travel a known distance (e.g. clap/echo method or oscilloscope with two microphones)
Calculate speed = distance/time, repeat and average to reduce random error

nodes.label: Method to measure the speed of ripples on a water surface
nodes.objective: Describe a method to measure the speed of ripples on a water surface.
essentialPoints: Measure wavelength and frequency of ripples in a ripple tank using a strobe/ruler
Use v = fλ, or time ripple travel over a measured distance directly

nodes.label: Relating changes in velocity, frequency and wavelength when sound changes medium (Physics only)
nodes.objective: Show how changes in velocity, frequency and wavelength are inter-related when sound passes from one medium to another.
essentialPoints: Frequency stays constant across a boundary between media
Velocity changes with medium, so wavelength must change proportionally (v = fλ)

nodes.label: Ultrasound waves: definition and reflection at boundaries (Physics only, HT only)
nodes.objective: Define ultrasound as sound above the upper limit of human hearing that partially reflects at boundaries between media.
essentialPoints: Ultrasound has frequency higher than the upper limit of human hearing
Ultrasound is partially reflected at a boundary between two different media

nodes.label: Specular vs diffuse reflection
nodes.objective: Distinguish specular reflection from a smooth surface and diffuse reflection (scattering) from a rough surface.
essentialPoints: Specular reflection: reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction
Diffuse reflection: scattering caused by reflection from a rough surface

nodes.label: Transparent and translucent objects
nodes.objective: Distinguish transparent and translucent objects as those that transmit light.
essentialPoints: Objects that transmit light are either transparent (clear, minimal scattering) or translucent (scatters light passing through)

nodes.label: Magnetic field strength and direction
nodes.objective: Describe how field strength varies with distance and how field direction is defined.
essentialPoints: Field strength depends on distance from the magnet and is strongest at the poles
Field direction at a point is the direction of force on a north pole placed there
Field lines point from north to south pole of a magnet

nodes.label: Magnetic field around a current-carrying wire
nodes.objective: Describe the magnetic field produced around a current-carrying conductor.
essentialPoints: A current flowing through a wire produces a magnetic field around it
Field strength depends on the current and the distance from the wire
This magnetic effect of current can be demonstrated experimentally (e.g. with iron filings or a compass)

nodes.label: Equilibrium between gravitational collapse and radiation/fusion expansion in a star
nodes.objective: Explain how a main-sequence star remains stable due to a balance of forces.
essentialPoints: Fusion energy creates outward pressure (expansion)
Gravity pulls inward (collapse)
Star is stable while these two effects balance

nodes.label: HT: For a stable orbit, radius must change if speed changes
nodes.objective: Explain qualitatively that maintaining a stable orbit requires the orbital radius to change if the orbital speed changes.
essentialPoints: A given orbital radius corresponds to a particular stable orbital speed for a given central mass
If speed increases, a larger radius is needed to remain in a stable orbit (and vice versa)

nodes.label: Red-shift as evidence for an expanding universe
nodes.objective: Explain how the relationship between galaxy speed and distance provides evidence that the universe is expanding.
essentialPoints: Galaxies further away recede faster, in all directions
This pattern is evidence that space itself is expanding, not just objects moving through static space

nodes.label: Health and safety: hazards and risk reduction
nodes.objective: Identify hazards in practical contexts and suggest methods to reduce risk of harm.
essentialPoints: A hazard is a source of potential harm; a risk is the chance of that harm occurring
Practical risks can be reduced by specific precautions (e.g. insulation, eye protection, safe handling)

nodes.label: Reading and recording measurements from a scale
nodes.objective: Make and record observations and measurements accurately using a range of apparatus, reading scales correctly.
essentialPoints: Measurements must be read to the resolution of the instrument's scale
Recorded values should include appropriate units and significant figures

nodes.label: AT2: Constructing electrical circuits from circuit diagrams
nodes.objective: Use circuit diagrams to construct and check series and parallel circuits, including ammeters and voltmeters.
essentialPoints: Circuit symbols represent specific components and must be connected as shown in the diagram
Ammeters are connected in series and voltmeters in parallel with the component being measured

nodes.label: Using standard form for very large or small numbers
nodes.objective: Recognise and use expressions in standard form (a × 10^n).
essentialPoints: Standard form expresses a number as a value between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten
Standard form is used to represent very large or very small physical quantities concisely

nodes.label: Comparing power outputs of devices doing the same task at different rates
nodes.objective: Give examples illustrating the definition of power, e.g. comparing two motors lifting the same weight at different speeds
essentialPoints: Two motors lifting the same weight through the same height transfer the same energy, but the faster one has greater power

nodes.label: Distinguishing renewable from non-renewable energy resources
nodes.objective: Classify each named energy resource as renewable or non-renewable
essentialPoints: Fossil fuels and nuclear fuel are non-renewable
Bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, tides, the Sun and water waves are renewable

nodes.label: Applying GPE and KE equations to analyse falling/rolling objects (energy transfer efficiency)
nodes.objective: Use measured height and speed data to calculate GPE lost and KE gained and compare the two values
essentialPoints: Calculate GPE lost using Ep = mgh from measured height
Calculate KE gained using Ek = 0.5mv^2 from measured speed
Compare the two calculated energies to assess energy transfer/dissipation

nodes.label: Reducing unwanted energy transfers using lubrication
nodes.objective: Explain how lubrication reduces unwanted energy transfers due to friction
essentialPoints: Lubrication reduces friction between surfaces, reducing the energy dissipated as heat/sound

nodes.label: Reducing unwanted energy transfers using thermal insulation
nodes.objective: Explain how thermal insulation reduces unwanted energy transfer by heating/cooling
essentialPoints: Thermal insulation reduces the rate of energy transfer to/from a system by heating, reducing wasted energy

nodes.label: Equation: charge flow = current × time (Q=It)
nodes.objective: Recall and apply Q = It
essentialPoints: charge flow (C) = current (A) × time (s)
Q = It

nodes.label: Current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop
nodes.objective: State that current is conserved around a single closed loop
essentialPoints: A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop

nodes.label: Current depends on resistance and potential difference
nodes.objective: Explain how current through a component depends on its resistance and the pd across it
essentialPoints: The current through a component depends on both the resistance and the pd across it
The greater the resistance, the smaller the current for a given pd

nodes.label: Direct and alternating potential difference
nodes.objective: Explain the difference between direct and alternating potential difference
essentialPoints: Direct pd (dc) maintains current flow in one direction only
Alternating pd (ac) repeatedly reverses direction of current flow

nodes.label: Work is done when charge flows in a circuit
nodes.objective: State that electrical work is done when charge flows round a circuit
essentialPoints: Work is done when charge flows in a circuit
This work is the mechanism by which electrical energy is transferred

nodes.label: Drawing the electric field pattern for an isolated charged sphere
nodes.objective: Draw the electric field pattern for an isolated charged sphere
essentialPoints: Field lines are drawn radiating from (or into) an isolated charged sphere, evenly spaced close to the sphere and spreading out further away

nodes.label: Force on a second charged object placed in a field
nodes.objective: Explain that a second charged object in a field experiences a force which strengthens as separation decreases
essentialPoints: A second charged object placed in the field experiences a force
The force gets stronger as the distance between the objects decreases

nodes.label: Specific heat capacity equation: ΔE = mcΔθ
nodes.objective: State and apply the equation change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change.
essentialPoints: ΔE = m c Δθ
ΔE in J, m in kg, c in J/kg°C, Δθ in °C

nodes.label: RP1 procedure: measuring temperature rise from energy input (work done/electrical) to determine specific heat capacity
nodes.objective: Carry out an experiment linking the decrease of one energy store (or work done) to a measured temperature rise in a material.
essentialPoints: Measure mass of the material sample using a balance
Supply a known amount of energy (electrical heater with known power and time, or work done) to the material
Measure the resulting temperature rise using a thermometer/temperature probe

nodes.label: Specific latent heat: definition
nodes.objective: Define specific latent heat as the energy required to change the state of one kilogram of a substance with no change in temperature.
essentialPoints: Specific latent heat is energy per kg needed to change state at constant temperature

nodes.label: Explaining how increasing volume decreases gas pressure at constant temperature
nodes.objective: Use the particle model to explain how increasing the volume of a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature decreases its pressure.
essentialPoints: Larger volume means molecules travel further between wall collisions
This reduces collision frequency on the walls, reducing pressure

nodes.label: Isotopes
nodes.objective: Define isotopes as atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, and relate this to atomic/mass number notation.
essentialPoints: Isotopes: same atomic number (protons), different neutron number
Different isotopes of an element have different mass numbers
Represented using standard nuclide notation (mass number, atomic number, symbol)

nodes.label: Chadwick's discovery of the neutron
nodes.objective: State that Chadwick's experimental work provided evidence for neutrons in the nucleus, about 20 years after acceptance of the nucleus.
essentialPoints: Chadwick's experimental work provided evidence for neutrons in the nucleus
This occurred about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted

nodes.label: Weight and mass are directly proportional
nodes.objective: Recognise that weight is directly proportional to mass for a given gravitational field strength.
essentialPoints: W ∝ m when g is constant
Use the ∝ symbol to express this relationship

nodes.label: Measuring weight with a newtonmeter
nodes.objective: Know that weight is measured using a calibrated spring-balance (newtonmeter).
essentialPoints: A newtonmeter is a calibrated spring balance used to measure force/weight

nodes.label: Resolving a force into two components (HT)
nodes.objective: Resolve a single force into two components acting at right angles using scale vector diagrams.
essentialPoints: A single force can be resolved into two perpendicular components with the same combined effect
Use scale vector diagrams to find magnitude and direction of resultant/components

nodes.label: Work done equation: W = Fs
nodes.objective: Recall and apply work done = force × distance moved along the line of action of the force.
essentialPoints: work done (J) = force (N) × distance moved along line of action (m)
1 joule = 1 newton-metre; can convert between Nm and J

nodes.label: Moment of a force equation: M = Fd
nodes.objective: Recall and apply moment = force × perpendicular distance from pivot to line of action.
essentialPoints: moment (Nm) = force (N) × perpendicular distance from pivot (m)

nodes.label: Hooke's law: extension proportional to force
nodes.objective: State that extension is directly proportional to force applied, provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.
essentialPoints: Extension ∝ force, up to the limit of proportionality
Beyond this limit the relationship is no longer proportional

nodes.label: Pressure due to a column of liquid: p = hρg (HT)
nodes.objective: Recall and apply pressure = height of column × density of liquid × gravitational field strength, and explain why pressure increases with depth and density.
essentialPoints: pressure (Pa) = height of column (m) × density (kg/m³) × g (N/kg)
Pressure at a point increases with the height of liquid above it and with the liquid's density
Can calculate pressure differences at different depths

nodes.label: Explaining why atmospheric pressure decreases with height
nodes.objective: Explain why atmospheric pressure varies with height above a surface in terms of colliding air molecules.
essentialPoints: Air molecules colliding with a surface create atmospheric pressure
The weight/number of air molecules above a surface decreases with increasing height, so atmospheric pressure decreases with height

nodes.label: Instantaneous speed from tangent to distance-time graph (HT)
nodes.objective: Determine the instantaneous speed of an accelerating object by drawing a tangent to a distance-time graph and measuring its gradient.
essentialPoints: For an accelerating object, speed at an instant is found from the gradient of a tangent drawn at that point

nodes.label: Estimating and interpreting stopping distance vs speed
nodes.objective: Estimate how emergency stopping distance varies with speed and interpret graphs of speed against stopping distance for different vehicles.
essentialPoints: Estimate stopping distances across a typical range of speeds
Read and interpret graphs relating speed to stopping distance for different vehicles

nodes.label: Reaction time and factors affecting it
nodes.objective: Know typical reaction time values and describe factors affecting a driver's reaction time.
essentialPoints: Typical reaction times range from 0.2 s to 0.9 s
Tiredness, drugs, alcohol and distractions can increase reaction time

nodes.label: Factors affecting braking distance: road, weather, vehicle condition
nodes.objective: Explain how adverse road/weather conditions and poor vehicle condition (brakes/tyres) affect braking distance and safety implications.
essentialPoints: Wet or icy road conditions increase braking distance
Poor condition of brakes or tyres increases braking distance
These factors have implications for road safety

nodes.label: Estimating magnitudes of everyday accelerations
nodes.objective: Estimate the magnitude of accelerations in everyday situations.
essentialPoints: Use knowledge of typical speeds and times to estimate realistic acceleration values

nodes.label: Velocity-time graphs and gradient as acceleration
nodes.objective: Draw velocity-time graphs from measurements and interpret gradient as acceleration.
essentialPoints: A velocity-time graph can be drawn from measured data
The gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration

nodes.label: Uniform acceleration equation: v² − u² = 2as
nodes.objective: Recall and apply v² − u² = 2as for uniformly accelerated motion.
essentialPoints: (final velocity)² − (initial velocity)² = 2 × acceleration × distance
Applies only to uniform acceleration

nodes.label: Inertia (HT)
nodes.objective: Define inertia as the tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or uniform motion.
essentialPoints: Inertia is the tendency of an object to stay at rest or keep moving at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force

nodes.label: Newton's Second Law and F = ma
nodes.objective: State Newton's Second Law and recall/apply resultant force = mass × acceleration.
essentialPoints: Acceleration is proportional to resultant force and inversely proportional to mass
resultant force (N) = mass (kg) × acceleration (m/s²)

nodes.label: Conservation of momentum (HT)
nodes.objective: State and apply the principle that in a closed system, total momentum before an event equals total momentum after.
essentialPoints: In a closed system, total momentum before an event equals total momentum after the event
Use momentum conservation to describe and explain collisions

nodes.label: Investigating collisions between trolleys to measure momentum (HT)
nodes.objective: Investigate collisions between laboratory trolleys using light gates, data loggers or ticker timers to measure and record data for momentum calculations.
essentialPoints: Set up trolleys with light gates/ticker timers to measure velocities before and after collision
