Record mass and velocity data to test conservation of momentum

nodes.label: Eyes only detect visible light: a limited range of the EM spectrum
nodes.objective: State that human eyes only detect visible light, a limited range of the EM spectrum.
essentialPoints: Human eyes only detect the visible light part of the EM spectrum

nodes.label: Absorption, transmission, refraction and reflection of EM waves vary with wavelength (HT only)
nodes.objective: State that different substances absorb, transmit, refract or reflect EM waves in ways that vary with wavelength.
essentialPoints: How a substance absorbs, transmits, refracts or reflects EM radiation depends on the wavelength of the radiation

nodes.label: EM waves generated/absorbed by changes in atoms and nuclei
nodes.objective: State that changes in atoms and nuclei can generate or absorb EM waves over a wide frequency range, with gamma rays originating from nuclear changes.
essentialPoints: Changes in electron energy levels in atoms can generate or absorb EM waves
Gamma rays specifically originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom

nodes.label: Application: radio waves for television and radio
nodes.objective: State that radio waves are used for television and radio broadcasting.
essentialPoints: Radio waves are used for television and radio transmission

nodes.label: Application: microwaves for satellite communication and cooking
nodes.objective: State that microwaves are used for satellite communications and cooking food.
essentialPoints: Microwaves are used for satellite communications
Microwaves are used to cook food

nodes.label: Application: infrared for heaters, cooking and cameras
nodes.objective: State that infrared is used in electrical heaters, cooking food and infrared cameras.
essentialPoints: Infrared used in electrical heaters and cooking food
Infrared used in infrared cameras

nodes.label: Application: visible light for fibre optic communication
nodes.objective: State that visible light is used for fibre optic communications.
essentialPoints: Visible light is used for fibre optic communication

nodes.label: Application: ultraviolet for lamps and sun tanning
nodes.objective: State that ultraviolet is used for energy efficient lamps and sun tanning.
essentialPoints: UV used in energy efficient lamps
UV used for sun tanning

nodes.label: Application: X-rays and gamma rays for medical imaging and treatment
nodes.objective: State that X-rays and gamma rays are used for medical imaging and treatments.
essentialPoints: X-rays and gamma rays used for medical imaging
X-rays and gamma rays used for medical treatments

nodes.label: Colours of visible light have specific wavelength/frequency bands
nodes.objective: State that each colour in the visible spectrum has its own narrow band of wavelength and frequency.
essentialPoints: Each colour of visible light corresponds to a narrow band of wavelength and frequency

nodes.label: Radio wave absorption inducing oscillations in a circuit (HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain that absorbed radio waves can create an alternating current in a circuit with the same frequency as the radio wave.
essentialPoints: When radio waves are absorbed by a circuit, they can induce an alternating current of the same frequency as the wave

nodes.label: Hazards of ultraviolet radiation to the body
nodes.objective: Describe the hazardous effects of ultraviolet radiation on human tissue.
essentialPoints: UV can cause skin to age prematurely
UV increases the risk of skin cancer

nodes.label: RP10 procedure: investigating infrared absorption/radiation vs surface type
nodes.objective: Carry out an investigation into how the amount of infrared radiation absorbed or radiated by a surface depends on the nature of that surface (e.g. Leslie's cube).
essentialPoints: Compare identical containers/surfaces (e.g. matt black, shiny, white) exposed to or emitting infrared radiation
Use a thermometer or infrared detector to measure temperature change over a fixed time for each surface
Control variables such as distance from source, starting temperature, and exposure time

nodes.label: Perfect black body: definition
nodes.objective: Define a perfect black body as an object that absorbs all incident radiation, without reflecting or transmitting any.
essentialPoints: A perfect black body absorbs all radiation incident on it
It does not reflect or transmit any radiation

nodes.label: RP8 application: calculating wave speed from ripple tank/solid data
nodes.objective: Use measured frequency and wavelength data from RP8 to calculate wave speed using v = fλ.
essentialPoints: Substitute measured f and λ into v = fλ to find speed
Compare calculated speed with directly-timed speed and evaluate agreement

nodes.label: Using ultrasound reflection time for detection and imaging (Physics only, HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain how measuring the time for ultrasound reflections to return allows the distance to a boundary to be found, enabling medical and industrial imaging.
essentialPoints: Time delay between transmitted pulse and reflected echo is used to calculate distance to the boundary
This allows imaging of internal structures for medical and industrial uses

nodes.label: Procedure: plotting a magnetic field pattern using a compass
nodes.objective: Describe the procedure for plotting the field pattern of a bar magnet using a plotting compass.
essentialPoints: Place a compass near the magnet and mark the direction it points
Move the compass along the field line, marking successive positions, and join the marks
Repeat from different starting points to build up the full field pattern

nodes.label: Compass behaviour as evidence for Earth's magnetic core
nodes.objective: Explain how the behaviour of a compass provides evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic.
essentialPoints: A compass contains a small bar magnet that aligns with a magnetic field
A compass needle points in the direction of the Earth's magnetic field
This behaviour is evidence that the Earth's core must be magnetic

nodes.label: The generator effect: induced potential difference and current (HT only)
nodes.objective: Describe the generator effect: induced pd/current from relative motion or changing magnetic field.
essentialPoints: A potential difference is induced across a conductor if it moves relative to a magnetic field, or if the magnetic field around it changes
If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, a current is induced
This is called the generator effect

nodes.label: Application: drawing the field pattern for a straight current-carrying wire
nodes.objective: Draw the magnetic field pattern for a straight wire carrying a current, showing direction.
essentialPoints: Concentric circles around the wire represent the field
Direction of the field reverses if current direction reverses (right-hand grip rule convention)

nodes.label: Solenoid: shape and field strength
nodes.objective: Explain how shaping a wire into a solenoid affects the magnetic field.
essentialPoints: Shaping a wire into a solenoid increases the strength of the magnetic field
The field inside a solenoid is strong and uniform
The field pattern around a solenoid resembles that of a bar magnet

nodes.label: The motor effect
nodes.objective: Describe the motor effect: force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
essentialPoints: When a current-carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field, the magnet and conductor exert a force on each other
This is called the motor effect

nodes.label: Life cycle of a star the size of the Sun
nodes.objective: Describe the life cycle stages of a star similar in mass to the Sun.
essentialPoints: Nebula -> main sequence star (stable) -> red giant
Red giant -> white dwarf -> black dwarf

nodes.label: Life cycle of a star much more massive than the Sun
nodes.objective: Describe the life cycle stages of a massive star.
essentialPoints: Nebula -> main sequence star (stable) -> red super giant
Red super giant -> supernova -> neutron star or black hole (depending on mass)

nodes.label: How red-shift evidence supports the Big Bang model
nodes.objective: Explain how the observation of an expanding universe (via red-shift) supports the Big Bang theory.
essentialPoints: An expanding universe implies that, going backwards in time, everything was once concentrated in a small region
This is consistent with the Big Bang theory's starting conditions

nodes.label: 1998 supernova observations: accelerating recession of distant galaxies
nodes.objective: State that observations of supernovae since 1998 suggest distant galaxies are receding at an increasing rate.
essentialPoints: Observations of supernovae since 1998 show distant galaxies receding ever faster
This suggests the rate of expansion of the universe is increasing (accelerating)

nodes.label: AT8 (physics only): Using ray boxes, mirrors, lenses and protractors for optics
nodes.objective: Use a ray box, protractor, mirrors, and lenses to measure angles of incidence, reflection and refraction, and to trace ray paths.
essentialPoints: A ray box produces a narrow visible beam of light for tracing on paper
A protractor measures angles of incidence, reflection and refraction relative to the normal

nodes.label: Constructing and interpreting tables, bar charts and histograms
nodes.objective: Present observations and data using frequency tables, bar charts and histograms.
essentialPoints: Frequency tables organise raw data into categories or class intervals
Bar charts and histograms visually represent frequency data for interpretation

nodes.label: Using appropriate significant figures
nodes.objective: Express calculated and measured values to an appropriate number of significant figures.
essentialPoints: The number of significant figures in an answer should reflect the precision of the data used
Rounding too early or reporting excess figures misrepresents precision

nodes.label: Calculating arithmetic mean and range
nodes.objective: Find the arithmetic mean and range of a set of repeated measurements.
essentialPoints: Mean is the sum of values divided by the number of values
Range is the difference between the largest and smallest value, used as a measure of spread

nodes.label: AT1: Using measuring cylinders, thermometers, and length instruments
nodes.objective: Use rulers, measuring cylinders, and thermometers correctly to measure length, volume and temperature.
essentialPoints: Length is measured using a ruler with the eye positioned perpendicular to avoid parallax error
Volumes are read at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus
Temperature is read from a thermometer scale to its stated resolution

nodes.label: Order of magnitude calculations
nodes.objective: Make order of magnitude estimates and comparisons using powers of ten.
essentialPoints: An order of magnitude estimate rounds a quantity to the nearest power of ten
Comparing orders of magnitude allows quick estimation of scale differences

nodes.label: Interconverting units
nodes.objective: Convert a quantity between different units, including using prefixes and standard form.
essentialPoints: Converting units requires multiplying or dividing by the appropriate conversion factor
Prefix values must be applied consistently when converting between unit sizes

nodes.label: Reliability of different energy resources
nodes.objective: Understand why some energy resources are more reliable than others
essentialPoints: Fossil fuels and nuclear provide reliable, on-demand power
Wind, solar and tidal are intermittent/weather- or time-dependent and thus less reliable

nodes.label: Environmental impact of using different energy resources
nodes.objective: Describe the environmental impact arising from the use of different energy resources
essentialPoints: Fossil fuel use releases greenhouse gases (e.g. CO2) contributing to global warming, and pollutants causing acid rain
Nuclear fuel use produces radioactive waste requiring careful storage/disposal
Renewables (wind, hydro, tidal, solar) can affect habitats/landscapes but produce no direct emissions during use

nodes.label: Thermal conductivity: higher conductivity means faster energy transfer by conduction
nodes.objective: State that the higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across it
essentialPoints: The higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction
Students do not need to know the formal definition of thermal conductivity

nodes.label: RP2 procedure: measuring temperature change over time for materials with different insulation
nodes.objective: Carry out the required practical investigating the effectiveness of different materials as thermal insulators
essentialPoints: Set up identical containers of hot water insulated with different materials (or thicknesses)
Measure and record temperature at regular time intervals for each set-up
Control variables such as starting temperature, volume of water and surface area

nodes.label: (HT only) Ways to increase the efficiency of an intended energy transfer
nodes.objective: Describe methods used to increase the efficiency of an intended energy transfer, such as lubrication and insulation, in the context of reducing dissipation
essentialPoints: Reducing friction (e.g. lubrication) reduces energy dissipated to unwanted stores, increasing useful output
Reducing unwanted energy transfer by heating (e.g. insulation) increases the proportion of useful energy transfer

nodes.label: Series circuits: same current through each component
nodes.objective: State that current is the same through each component in series
essentialPoints: For components connected in series, there is the same current through each component

nodes.label: Equation: potential difference = current × resistance (V=IR)
nodes.objective: Recall and apply V = IR
essentialPoints: potential difference (V) = current (A) × resistance (Ω)
V = IR

nodes.label: Equation: power = potential difference × current (P=VI)
nodes.objective: Recall and apply P = VI
essentialPoints: power (W) = potential difference (V) × current (A)
P = VI

nodes.label: UK mains supply: 230 V, 50 Hz ac
nodes.objective: State the UK domestic mains supply frequency and voltage
essentialPoints: Mains electricity is an ac supply
In the UK, domestic supply has a frequency of 50 Hz and is about 230 V

nodes.label: Equation: energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference (E=QV)
nodes.objective: Recall and apply E = QV
essentialPoints: energy transferred (J) = charge flow (C) × potential difference (V)
E = QV

nodes.label: Electric field explains non-contact force and electrostatic phenomena
nodes.objective: Explain how the concept of an electric field explains non-contact forces between charges and phenomena such as sparking
essentialPoints: The electric field concept explains the non-contact force between charged objects
It also explains other electrostatic phenomena such as sparking, when the field is strong enough to ionise air

nodes.label: Calculating energy change, mass, specific heat capacity or temperature change using ΔE = mcΔθ
nodes.objective: Rearrange and apply ΔE = mcΔθ to calculate any one variable given the others.
essentialPoints: Rearrange equation to solve for m, c or Δθ
Substitute values with correct units to find ΔE

nodes.label: RP1 evaluation: sources of error in specific heat capacity measurement
nodes.objective: Evaluate the RP1 method for sources of error, such as heat loss to the surroundings, and suggest improvements.
essentialPoints: Heat loss to surroundings causes measured c to be too high (systematic error)
Insulating the sample and using a lid reduces heat loss
Delay in thermometer response affects accuracy of temperature readings

nodes.label: Specific latent heat of fusion vs specific latent heat of vaporisation
nodes.objective: Distinguish between specific latent heat of fusion (solid to liquid) and specific latent heat of vaporisation (liquid to vapour).
essentialPoints: Latent heat of fusion applies to solid-liquid change of state
Latent heat of vaporisation applies to liquid-vapour change of state

nodes.label: Specific latent heat equation: E = mL
nodes.objective: State and apply the equation energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat.
essentialPoints: E = m L
E in J, m in kg, L in J/kg

nodes.label: Distinguishing specific heat capacity from specific latent heat
nodes.objective: Distinguish between specific heat capacity (temperature change, no state change) and specific latent heat (state change, no temperature change).
essentialPoints: Specific heat capacity relates to energy causing temperature change
Specific latent heat relates to energy causing a change of state at constant temperature

nodes.label: Boyle's Law equation: pV = constant
nodes.objective: State the equation pressure × volume = constant for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature.
essentialPoints: pV = constant for fixed mass of gas at constant temperature
p in pascals (Pa), V in cubic metres (m³)

nodes.label: Radioactive decay as a random process
nodes.objective: Describe unstable nuclei giving out radiation to become more stable, and that this is random.
essentialPoints: Some nuclei are unstable and emit radiation to become more stable
Radioactive decay is a random process (cannot predict which nucleus decays next or when)

nodes.label: Background radiation and its sources
nodes.objective: Describe background radiation and its natural and man-made sources.
essentialPoints: Background radiation is present around us all the time
Natural sources: rocks, cosmic rays from space
Man-made sources: fallout from nuclear weapons testing, nuclear accidents

nodes.label: Nuclear fission: definition
nodes.objective: Define nuclear fission as the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus (e.g. uranium or plutonium).
essentialPoints: Fission = splitting of a large, unstable nucleus (e.g. uranium, plutonium)

nodes.label: Energy transfer associated with work done
nodes.objective: Describe the energy transfer involved when work is done on an object.
essentialPoints: Doing work on an object transfers energy to or from that object's energy stores

nodes.label: Balancing clockwise and anticlockwise moments
nodes.objective: Calculate an unknown force or distance for a balanced object using the principle that total clockwise moment equals total anticlockwise moment.
essentialPoints: For a balanced object, total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment about the pivot
Use this to solve for unknown force or distance

nodes.label: Levers and gears transmitting rotational effects
nodes.objective: Explain how simple levers and gear systems transmit the rotational effects of forces.
essentialPoints: A lever transmits and can amplify the turning effect of a force about a pivot
A gear system transmits rotational effects between meshed gears, changing force/speed of rotation

nodes.label: Spring constant equation: F = ke
nodes.objective: Recall and apply force = spring constant × extension, also applicable to compression.
essentialPoints: force (N) = spring constant (N/m) × extension (m)
Same equation applies to compression, with e as compression

nodes.label: RP6 procedure: investigating force vs extension for a spring
nodes.objective: Carry out the procedure to measure extension of a spring for a range of applied forces.
essentialPoints: Measure natural length of spring, then add known masses/forces and measure new length
Calculate extension for each force and repeat for reliability
Plot force against extension

nodes.label: Upthrust and floating/sinking (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain that a submerged object experiences greater pressure on its bottom than top surface, creating an upward resultant force (upthrust), and describe factors influencing floating and sinking.
essentialPoints: Greater pressure on the bottom surface than the top surface of a submerged object creates an upward resultant force called upthrust
An object floats if upthrust equals or exceeds its weight; sinks if weight exceeds upthrust
Factors influencing floating/sinking include object density relative to fluid density

nodes.label: Measuring human reaction time (e.g. ruler drop test)
nodes.objective: Explain and carry out simple methods used to measure human reaction times, including the effect of distractions.
essentialPoints: Use a simple method (e.g. ruler drop test) to measure reaction time
Repeat measurements to test reliability and reduce anomalies

nodes.label: Area under velocity-time graph = distance/displacement (HT)
nodes.objective: Interpret the enclosed area under a velocity-time graph as distance travelled or displacement, including by counting squares.
essentialPoints: The area under a velocity-time graph represents distance travelled (or displacement)
For non-uniform (curved) sections, measure area by counting squares

nodes.label: Acceleration of free fall near Earth's surface
nodes.objective: Know that objects falling freely under gravity near Earth's surface accelerate at about 9.8 m/s².
essentialPoints: Free-falling objects near Earth's surface accelerate at approximately 9.8 m/s²

nodes.label: Inertial mass (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain inertial mass as a measure of how difficult it is to change an object's velocity, defined as the ratio of force to acceleration.
essentialPoints: Inertial mass measures how difficult it is to change an object's velocity
Inertial mass = force / acceleration

nodes.label: Estimating speeds, accelerations and forces for road transport
nodes.objective: Estimate the speed, acceleration and forces involved in large accelerations for everyday road transport, using the approximation symbol.
essentialPoints: Use F=ma and typical vehicle data to estimate realistic forces/accelerations
Recognise and use the approximation symbol ~

nodes.label: RP7 procedure: investigating force, mass and acceleration
nodes.objective: Carry out an investigation into the effect of varying force on acceleration for constant mass, and varying mass on acceleration for constant force.
essentialPoints: Use a trolley/track setup, varying the accelerating force while keeping mass constant, and measuring acceleration
Repeat while varying the mass and keeping force constant
Use light gates/ticker timer/data logger to record motion data

nodes.label: Force as rate of change of momentum: F = mΔv/Δt (physics only, HT)
nodes.objective: Derive and apply F = mΔv/Δt by combining F=ma and a=Δv/Δt, understanding force equals rate of change of momentum.
essentialPoints: Combining F=ma and a=Δv/Δt gives F = mΔv/Δt
Force equals the rate of change of momentum

nodes.label: Calculations involving conservation of momentum in collisions (physics only, HT)
nodes.objective: Complete calculations involving momentum conservation in events such as collisions between two objects.
essentialPoints: Apply p = mv and conservation of momentum to calculate unknown masses, velocities in collisions

nodes.label: Refraction caused by change in wave velocity between substances (HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain that refraction occurs because of the difference in wave velocity between different substances.
essentialPoints: Refraction results from the wave changing speed as it crosses a boundary between media of different density/optical properties

nodes.label: Ionising hazards of X-rays and gamma rays
nodes.objective: Describe X-rays and gamma rays as ionising radiation that can cause gene mutation and cancer.
essentialPoints: X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation
They can cause mutation of genes and cancer

nodes.label: Explaining why radio waves suit their applications (HT only)
nodes.objective: Give a brief explanation of why radio waves are suitable for television and radio transmission.
essentialPoints: Radio waves travel long distances and diffract around obstacles/hills, and are not readily absorbed by the atmosphere

nodes.label: Explaining why microwaves suit their applications (HT only)
nodes.objective: Give a brief explanation of why microwaves are suitable for satellite communication and cooking.
essentialPoints: Certain microwave wavelengths pass through the atmosphere, suiting satellite links
Other microwave wavelengths are absorbed by water molecules in food, heating it

nodes.label: Explaining why infrared suits its applications (HT only)
nodes.objective: Give a brief explanation of why infrared is suitable for heaters, cooking and cameras.
essentialPoints: Infrared is readily absorbed by materials/skin, transferring energy as heat, suiting heaters and cooking
Infrared is emitted by all warm objects, allowing thermal imaging cameras to detect them

nodes.label: How colour filters work
nodes.objective: Explain that colour filters work by absorbing certain wavelengths and transmitting others.
essentialPoints: A filter absorbs certain wavelengths of light and transmits the remaining wavelengths, giving the transmitted colour

nodes.label: Colour of an opaque object from differential reflection/absorption
nodes.objective: Explain how the colour of an opaque object is determined by which wavelengths are more strongly reflected versus absorbed.
essentialPoints: The colour seen is determined by which wavelengths are most strongly reflected; other wavelengths are absorbed
An object appears white if all wavelengths are reflected equally, and black if all are absorbed

nodes.label: Explaining why ultraviolet suits its applications (HT only)
nodes.objective: Give a brief explanation of why ultraviolet is suitable for energy efficient lamps and sun tanning.
essentialPoints: Fluorescent coatings in lamps absorb UV and re-emit it as visible light efficiently
UV causes the skin to tan by stimulating melanin production

nodes.label: RP10 application: relating surface type to IR absorption/emission results
nodes.objective: Interpret RP10 results to conclude how surface nature (colour, texture) affects infrared absorption and emission.
essentialPoints: Matt/dark surfaces absorb and emit infrared more effectively than shiny/light surfaces
Use recorded temperature changes to rank surfaces by absorbing/emitting ability

nodes.label: A good absorber is also a good emitter (perfect black body as best emitter)
nodes.objective: State that a good absorber of radiation is also a good emitter, so a perfect black body is the best possible emitter.
essentialPoints: A good absorber of radiation is also a good emitter
A perfect black body is therefore the best possible emitter of radiation

nodes.label: Echo sounding using high frequency sound (Physics only, HT only)
nodes.objective: Describe how echo sounding using high frequency sound waves detects objects and measures depth in deep water.
essentialPoints: High frequency sound pulses are sent down through water
Time for the echo to return from the sea bed/object is used to calculate depth/distance

nodes.label: Application: drawing the magnetic field pattern of a bar magnet
nodes.objective: Draw the field pattern of a bar magnet showing how strength and direction vary from point to point.
essentialPoints: Field lines drawn from N to S pole, closer together near poles (stronger field)
Direction shown by arrows on field lines
Spacing of lines indicates relative field strength at different points

nodes.label: Induced current opposes the change that produced it (HT only)
nodes.objective: State that an induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change.
essentialPoints: The magnetic field generated by an induced current opposes the change producing it (the motion of the conductor or the change in field)

nodes.label: Application: drawing the field pattern for a solenoid
nodes.objective: Draw the magnetic field pattern for a solenoid showing field direction.
essentialPoints: Field lines inside the solenoid are parallel and close together (uniform, strong)
Field lines outside resemble a bar magnet's field, curving from one end to the other
Direction of field lines follows from the current direction in the coils

nodes.label: Electromagnet: iron core increases solenoid field strength
nodes.objective: Explain how adding an iron core to a solenoid increases magnetic field strength to form an electromagnet.
essentialPoints: Adding an iron core increases the strength of a solenoid's magnetic field
An electromagnet is defined as a solenoid with an iron core

nodes.label: Fleming's left-hand rule (HT only)
nodes.objective: Use Fleming's left-hand rule to relate the directions of force, current and magnetic field.
essentialPoints: Fleming's left-hand rule represents the relative orientation of force, current and magnetic field
Thumb = force (thrust), first finger = field, second finger = current

nodes.label: Fusion processes in stars forming new (naturally occurring) elements
nodes.objective: Explain how fusion processes in stars during their life cycle lead to the formation of elements up to iron.
essentialPoints: Fusion of lighter nuclei in stars produces progressively heavier elements
This process continues through a star's life cycle stages, producing elements up to iron

nodes.label: How scientists use observations to develop and support theories (e.g. the Big Bang)
nodes.objective: Explain the process by which observations (such as red-shift) lead scientists to develop and support scientific theories like the Big Bang model.
essentialPoints: Scientists collect observational data (e.g. red-shift measurements of galaxies)
Theories are developed/refined to explain patterns in the data, and are tested against further observations

nodes.label: Unresolved questions: dark mass (dark matter) and dark energy
nodes.objective: State that dark matter and dark energy remain not fully understood aspects of the universe.
essentialPoints: Dark matter affects galaxies (e.g. bends light, holds galaxies together) but does not emit electromagnetic radiation, and its nature is not understood
Dark energy is a proposed explanation for the observed acceleration of the universe's expansion, and is not fully understood

nodes.label: Plotting two variables from data
nodes.objective: Plot two variables from experimental or other data on a graph with appropriate axes and scales.
essentialPoints: Independent variable is plotted on the x-axis, dependent on the y-axis
Axes must be labelled with quantity and unit, with sensible scales

nodes.label: Understanding mean, mode and median
nodes.objective: Understand and distinguish the statistical terms mean, mode and median.
essentialPoints: Mode is the most frequently occurring value
Median is the middle value when data is ordered

nodes.label: Estimating uncertainty using the range about the mean
nodes.objective: Represent distributions of results and estimate uncertainty using the range of measurements about the mean.
essentialPoints: Every measurement has some associated uncertainty
The range of repeated measurements about the mean can be used as an estimate of uncertainty

nodes.label: AT1: Using a stopwatch/timer for repeated readings
nodes.objective: Use a stopwatch or timer to measure time intervals, taking repeat readings to improve reliability.
essentialPoints: A stopwatch is started and stopped consistently at defined events to measure a time interval
Repeating timings and averaging reduces the effect of random error

nodes.label: AT5: Measuring forces and extension using a newtonmeter and ruler
nodes.objective: Use a newtonmeter to measure force and a ruler to measure the extension of a spring or material under load.
essentialPoints: A newtonmeter (spring balance) measures force directly in newtons
Extension is calculated as the difference between stretched length and natural (unstretched) length

nodes.label: AT7: Measuring energy changes/transfers using temperature and calorimetry apparatus
nodes.objective: Use thermometers, insulated containers and heaters to measure temperature changes associated with energy transfers.
essentialPoints: Temperature change over time is measured using a thermometer or temperature sensor while a known energy input is applied
Insulation is used to minimise unwanted energy transfer to the surroundings during the measurement

nodes.label: Making estimates of the results of calculations
nodes.objective: Make sensible estimates of the results of simple calculations without full computation.
essentialPoints: Estimation uses rounded values to quickly approximate a calculation's result
Estimates allow a check on whether a calculated answer is reasonable

nodes.label: Patterns and trends in the use of energy resources
nodes.objective: Explain patterns and trends in the use of energy resources over time, e.g. shift towards renewables
essentialPoints: Data on energy resource use over time can show trends such as increasing use of renewables and declining reliance on fossil fuels
Trends are influenced by factors such as cost, technology and policy

nodes.label: Science can identify environmental issues but not always resolve them due to political, social, ethical or economic factors
nodes.objective: Explain that science can identify environmental issues from energy resource use but political, social, ethical or economic considerations affect whether they are addressed
essentialPoints: Science can identify environmental issues arising from energy resource use
Addressing those issues is limited by political, social, ethical or economic considerations, not just scientific capability

nodes.label: Effect of wall thickness and thermal conductivity on the rate of cooling of a building
nodes.objective: Describe how the rate of cooling of a building is affected by the thickness and thermal conductivity of its walls
essentialPoints: Thicker walls reduce the rate of energy transfer (slower cooling)
Walls made of materials with lower thermal conductivity reduce the rate of cooling

nodes.label: AT1/AT5 practical: investigating thermal conductivity using rods of different materials
nodes.objective: Carry out an investigation comparing the rate of energy transfer through rods of different materials
essentialPoints: Heat one end of rods of different materials and observe/measure the rate at which heat travels along each (e.g. using wax/temperature sensors)
Compare results between materials to rank thermal conductivity

nodes.label: RP2 application: comparing insulating effectiveness and identifying factors affecting insulation
nodes.objective: Interpret temperature-time data to compare the effectiveness of different insulating materials and identify factors affecting insulation performance
essentialPoints: Compare rate of temperature fall between different insulating materials/thicknesses from graphs or tables
Relate results to thermal conductivity and thickness of the insulating material

nodes.label: RP3: constructing circuits to investigate resistance factors
nodes.objective: Set up and check circuits using circuit diagrams to investigate factors affecting resistance, including wire length and resistor combinations
essentialPoints: Use circuit diagrams to set up and check appropriate series/parallel circuits
Vary length of a wire at constant temperature and measure current/pd to find resistance
Set up combinations of resistors in series and in parallel and measure their resistance

nodes.label: Ohmic conductors: constant resistance
nodes.objective: Explain that ohmic conductors have constant resistance and directly proportional I-V relationship at constant temperature
essentialPoints: The current through an ohmic conductor at constant temperature is directly proportional to the pd across it
This means resistance remains constant as current changes

nodes.label: Circuit design for measuring resistance of a component
nodes.objective: Explain the design and use of a circuit to measure the resistance of a component by measuring current and pd
essentialPoints: A circuit measures current through and pd across a component using an ammeter and voltmeter
An appropriate circuit diagram is drawn using correct circuit symbols
Resistance is then calculated using V=IR

nodes.label: Series circuits: pd shared between components
nodes.objective: State that total pd is shared between components in series
essentialPoints: The total potential difference of the power supply is shared between the components in series

nodes.label: Parallel circuits: same pd across each component
nodes.objective: State that pd is the same across each branch in parallel
essentialPoints: For components connected in parallel, the potential difference across each component is the same

nodes.label: Equation: power = current² × resistance (P=I²R)
nodes.objective: Recall and apply P = I²R
essentialPoints: power (W) = current² (A²) × resistance (Ω)
P = I²R

nodes.label: Relating power transfer to energy changes over time
nodes.objective: Explain how power transfer in a circuit device relates to pd, current and energy changes over time
essentialPoints: Power transfer in any circuit device is related to the pd across it and the current through it
This power corresponds to the rate of energy transfer (energy change over time)

nodes.label: Three-core cable and wire colour coding
nodes.objective: Identify the three wires in mains cable and their colour coding
essentialPoints: Most electrical appliances connect to mains using three-core cable
Live wire is brown, neutral wire is blue, earth wire is green and yellow striped

nodes.label: RP1 application: calculating specific heat capacity from experimental data
nodes.objective: Use measured mass, energy supplied and temperature rise to calculate the specific heat capacity of a material.
essentialPoints: Rearrange ΔE = mcΔθ to find c = ΔE/(mΔθ)
Substitute experimental values to calculate specific heat capacity

nodes.label: Practical: measuring the latent heat of fusion of water
nodes.objective: Carry out an experiment to measure the specific latent heat of fusion of ice/water using a heater and measured mass of melted ice.
essentialPoints: Supply known electrical energy to melt ice using an immersion heater
Measure mass of ice melted over a measured time period
Account for a control experiment without the heater to correct for background melting
specRefs: AT5, latent heat of fusion practical

nodes.label: Calculating energy, mass or specific latent heat using E = mL
nodes.objective: Rearrange and apply E = mL to calculate energy, mass or specific latent heat given the other two quantities.
essentialPoints: Rearrange E = mL to solve for m or L
Substitute values with correct units to find E

nodes.label: Calculating pressure or volume changes using p1V1 = p2V2
nodes.objective: Apply pV = constant to calculate the change in pressure or volume of a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature.
essentialPoints: Use p1V1 = p2V2 to find an unknown pressure or volume
Rearrange the equation to isolate the required variable

nodes.label: Doing work on a gas increases its internal energy and can raise its temperature (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain how doing work on an enclosed gas (e.g. compressing it with a bicycle pump) increases its internal energy and can cause a temperature increase.
essentialPoints: Work done on the gas transfers energy to the gas particles, increasing internal energy
Increased internal energy can raise the gas's temperature
Example: compressing air in a bicycle pump makes it warmer

nodes.label: Activity and the becquerel
nodes.objective: Define activity as the rate at which unstable nuclei decay, measured in becquerel.
essentialPoints: Activity = rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays
Measured in becquerel (Bq)

nodes.label: Alpha particle: composition and nature
nodes.objective: Describe an alpha particle as two protons and two neutrons, equivalent to a helium nucleus.
essentialPoints: Alpha particle consists of 2 protons and 2 neutrons
Equivalent to a helium nucleus

nodes.label: Beta particle: origin and nature
nodes.objective: Describe a beta particle as a high-speed electron ejected from the nucleus when a neutron turns into a proton.
essentialPoints: Beta particle is a high-speed electron ejected from the nucleus
Emitted when a neutron changes into a proton

nodes.label: Gamma ray: nature
nodes.objective: Describe a gamma ray as electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus.
essentialPoints: Gamma ray is electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus

nodes.label: Neutron emission as nuclear radiation
nodes.objective: State that a neutron can be emitted as a type of nuclear radiation.
essentialPoints: A free neutron (n) can be emitted from an unstable nucleus

nodes.label: Radioactive contamination
nodes.objective: Define radioactive contamination as the unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on materials, and its hazard.
essentialPoints: Contamination = unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials
Hazard arises from the decay of the contaminating atoms themselves
Type of radiation emitted affects the level of hazard

nodes.label: Effect of occupation and location on radiation dose
nodes.objective: Explain how background radiation level and radiation dose may be affected by occupation and/or location.
essentialPoints: Certain jobs (e.g. nuclear industry, medical imaging) increase radiation exposure
Certain locations (e.g. altitude, geology) increase background radiation levels

nodes.label: Nuclear fusion: definition
nodes.objective: Define nuclear fusion as the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, with mass converted to energy.
essentialPoints: Fusion = joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus
Some mass may be converted into the energy of radiation during fusion

nodes.label: Work done against friction raises temperature
nodes.objective: Explain that work done against frictional forces causes a rise in temperature of an object.
essentialPoints: Work done against friction transfers energy to the thermal energy store, raising temperature

nodes.label: Linear vs non-linear force-extension relationships
nodes.objective: Describe the difference between a linear and non-linear relationship between force and extension, and calculate spring constant in linear cases.
essentialPoints: A linear relationship gives a straight-line graph (constant spring constant)
A non-linear relationship curves once limit of proportionality is exceeded
Spring constant can be calculated from gradient in the linear region

nodes.label: Elastic potential energy equation: Ee = ½ke²
nodes.objective: Recall and apply elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × extension² up to the limit of proportionality.
essentialPoints: Ee (J) = 0.5 × k (N/m) × e² (m²)
Only valid up to the limit of proportionality

nodes.label: Interpreting and evaluating reaction time data
nodes.objective: Interpret and evaluate measurements from reaction time experiments and evaluate the effect of factors on thinking distance from given data.
essentialPoints: Analyse collected reaction time data for patterns and reliability
Evaluate how factors like distraction affect thinking distance using given data

nodes.label: Terminal velocity of a falling object (physics only)
nodes.objective: Explain that a falling object accelerates due to gravity until resultant force is zero, reaching terminal velocity, and interpret related velocity-time graphs.
essentialPoints: An object falling through a fluid initially accelerates due to gravity
As speed increases, resistive force (e.g. air resistance/drag) increases until it balances weight, giving zero resultant force
At terminal velocity the object moves at constant speed

nodes.label: Interpreting force-mass-acceleration data from RP7
nodes.objective: Interpret RP7 results to confirm the relationships between force, mass and acceleration described by Newton's Second Law.
essentialPoints: Identify that acceleration is proportional to force at constant mass
Identify that acceleration is inversely proportional to mass at constant force

nodes.label: Explaining safety features using rate of change of momentum (physics only, HT)
nodes.objective: Explain safety features such as air bags, seat belts, crash mats, cycle helmets and cushioned playground surfaces in terms of rate of change of momentum.
essentialPoints: Safety features increase the time over which momentum changes, reducing the force experienced
Examples: air bags, seat belts, crash mats, cycle helmets, cushioned playground surfaces

nodes.label: Applying combined force, mass, velocity and acceleration equations (HT)
nodes.objective: Apply equations relating force, mass, velocity and acceleration together to explain how related changes are inter-related.
essentialPoints: Combine F=ma, a=Δv/Δt, p=mv and F=mΔv/Δt to solve multi-step problems relating these quantities

nodes.label: Ray diagrams for refraction at a boundary between media
nodes.objective: Construct ray diagrams to illustrate the refraction of a wave at the boundary between two different media.
essentialPoints: Draw incident ray bending towards/away from normal at the boundary depending on change in speed
Ray bends towards the normal when entering a denser medium (slower speed), away when leaving it

nodes.label: Wave front diagrams explaining refraction via change of speed (HT only)
nodes.objective: Use wave front diagrams to explain refraction in terms of the change of speed when a wave travels between media.
essentialPoints: Wavefronts change spacing/direction as speed changes when entering a new medium at an angle
This change in wavefront direction accounts for the bending of the ray (refraction)

nodes.label: Explaining why visible light suits fibre optic communication (HT only)
nodes.objective: Give a brief explanation of why visible light is suitable for fibre optic communication.
essentialPoints: Visible light can be transmitted along thin glass fibres with minimal absorption, carrying data over long distances by total internal reflection

nodes.label: Drawing conclusions from data on radiation exposure risks
nodes.objective: Draw conclusions from given data about the risks and consequences of exposure to ionising/UV radiation.
essentialPoints: Interpret dose-response data to assess relative risk of different exposures
Link magnitude of dose to likelihood/severity of harm described in data

nodes.label: Explaining why X-rays and gamma rays suit medical uses (HT only)
nodes.objective: Give a brief explanation of why X-rays and gamma rays are suitable for medical imaging and treatment.
essentialPoints: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by denser material like bone, allowing imaging
Gamma rays' ionising energy can be targeted to kill cancer cells in treatment

nodes.label: Effect of viewing objects through colour filters
nodes.objective: Explain the effect of viewing objects through filters, or the effect on light of passing through filters.
essentialPoints: A filter changes the apparent colour of an object by removing wavelengths from the light reaching the eye
An object's colour under a filter depends on whether the wavelengths it reflects are transmitted by the filter

nodes.label: Intensity and wavelength distribution of emitted radiation depend on temperature
nodes.objective: Explain that the intensity and wavelength distribution of radiation emitted by a body depends on its temperature.
essentialPoints: All bodies emit radiation across a range of wavelengths
Both the total intensity and the distribution of wavelengths emitted depend on the body's temperature

nodes.label: Factors affecting size and direction of induced pd/current (HT only)
nodes.objective: Recall the factors affecting the size and direction of induced potential difference/current.
essentialPoints: Size depends on factors such as speed of relative motion, strength of magnetic field, number of turns/coil orientation
Direction depends on the direction of motion (or field change) and the orientation of the field, reversing if either reverses

nodes.label: Interpreting diagrams of electromagnetic devices (physics only)
nodes.objective: Interpret diagrams of electromagnetic devices to explain how they work.
essentialPoints: Use knowledge of solenoids/electromagnets to explain the operation of devices shown in unfamiliar diagrams (e.g. relays, circuit breakers)

nodes.label: Transformer structure: primary and secondary coils on an iron core
nodes.objective: Describe the basic structure of a transformer.
essentialPoints: A basic transformer has a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core
Iron is used because it is easily magnetised
Laminations and eddy currents in the core are not required knowledge

nodes.label: Factors affecting the size of the force on a current-carrying conductor (HT only)
nodes.objective: Recall the factors affecting the size of the force on a conductor in a magnetic field.
essentialPoints: Force depends on the magnetic flux density, the current, and the length of conductor in the field

nodes.label: Electric motors (HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain how the motor effect causes rotation of a coil in an electric motor.
essentialPoints: A coil carrying a current in a magnetic field experiences forces that tend to rotate it
Forces on opposite sides of the coil act in opposite directions (using Fleming's left-hand rule), producing a turning effect
This is the basis of an electric motor

nodes.label: Moving-coil microphones (physics only, HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain how a moving-coil microphone uses the generator effect.
essentialPoints: Sound waves cause a diaphragm and attached coil to vibrate within a magnetic field
This changing motion of the coil in the field induces a varying current, matching the sound wave's pressure variations

nodes.label: Formation of elements heavier than iron and their distribution by supernova
nodes.objective: Explain that elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova explosion, which distributes all elements through the universe.
essentialPoints: Elements heavier than iron are only produced during a supernova explosion
The supernova explosion distributes elements throughout the universe, becoming raw material for new stars/planets

nodes.label: Translating data between graphical and numeric forms
nodes.objective: Convert data between tabular/numeric form and graphical representation.
essentialPoints: Values from a table can be read directly onto a graph and vice versa
Graphical trends can be described in words or numbers

nodes.label: Determining slope and intercept of a linear graph
nodes.objective: Determine the gradient and y-intercept of a linear graph and relate them to y = mx + c.
essentialPoints: Gradient is calculated as change in y divided by change in x between two points on the line
The y-intercept is the value of y where the line crosses the y-axis
y = mx + c represents a linear relationship where m is gradient and c is intercept

nodes.label: Finding the area between a curve and the x-axis
nodes.objective: Determine the physical significance of the area under a graph and measure it by counting squares.
essentialPoints: The area between a curve and the x-axis can represent a physical quantity (e.g. distance from a velocity-time graph)
Area under a curved graph can be estimated by counting the enclosed squares

nodes.label: Using scatter diagrams to identify correlation
nodes.objective: Use a scatter diagram to identify whether a correlation exists between two variables.
essentialPoints: A scatter diagram plots pairs of values to reveal a possible relationship
Correlation shown on a scatter diagram does not by itself prove causation

nodes.label: Accuracy and precision of measurements
nodes.objective: Distinguish accuracy (closeness to true value) from precision (closeness of clustering of repeated measurements).
essentialPoints: An accurate measurement is close to the true value
Measurements are precise if they cluster closely together, regardless of accuracy

nodes.label: AT3: Measuring distance, time and using light gates/motion sensors
nodes.objective: Measure distance and time using appropriate apparatus (including light gates and data loggers where used) to determine motion quantities.
essentialPoints: Distance travelled and corresponding time intervals are measured to calculate speed or acceleration
Light gates/data loggers can measure short time intervals more precisely than manual timing

nodes.label: AT4: Making observations of waves in a ripple tank or with a signal generator
nodes.objective: Use a ripple tank, signal generator, and oscilloscope/microphone to observe and measure wave properties such as frequency and wavelength.
essentialPoints: A ripple tank allows observation of wavefronts to measure wavelength directly
A signal generator and oscilloscope allow frequency and time period of a wave to be determined

nodes.label: AT6: Using detectors to measure radioactive emissions
nodes.objective: Use a Geiger-Muller tube/counter to detect and measure count rate of radioactive emissions, accounting for background radiation.
essentialPoints: A Geiger-Muller tube detects ionising radiation and a counter records count rate
Background radiation must be measured separately and accounted for when interpreting readings

nodes.label: Interpreting resistance data from wire length and resistor combination investigations
nodes.objective: Analyse and interpret data from RP3 to draw conclusions about resistance and wire length/resistor combinations
essentialPoints: Use collected I and V data to calculate resistance using V=IR
Identify the relationship between wire length and resistance from graphed data
Compare measured series/parallel combined resistances with calculated predictions

nodes.label: Filament lamp: resistance increases with temperature
nodes.objective: Explain that filament lamp resistance is non-constant and increases as filament temperature increases
essentialPoints: The resistance of a filament lamp is not constant, it changes with current
The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases

nodes.label: Diode: one-direction current, high reverse resistance
nodes.objective: Describe the non-ohmic behaviour of a diode
essentialPoints: Current through a diode flows in one direction only
The diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction

nodes.label: Thermistor: resistance decreases as temperature increases
nodes.objective: Describe the temperature-resistance relationship of a thermistor
essentialPoints: The resistance of a thermistor decreases as temperature increases

nodes.label: LDR: resistance decreases as light intensity increases
nodes.objective: Describe the light-resistance relationship of an LDR
essentialPoints: The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases

nodes.label: Series circuits: total resistance is the sum of resistances
nodes.objective: Recall and apply R_total = R1 + R2 for resistors in series
essentialPoints: The total resistance of two components in series is the sum of their resistances
R_total = R1 + R2

nodes.label: Parallel circuits: total current is the sum of branch currents
nodes.objective: State that total current in parallel equals the sum of currents in each branch
essentialPoints: The total current through the whole parallel circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components

nodes.label: Constructing and checking series and parallel circuits
nodes.objective: Use circuit diagrams to construct and check series and parallel circuits with common components
essentialPoints: Circuit diagrams can be used to build and verify circuits combining series and parallel sections with various components

nodes.label: Why the National Grid is an efficient way to transfer energy
nodes.objective: Explain why transmitting at high pd and low current improves efficiency of energy transfer in the National Grid
essentialPoints: Transmitting at high pd allows low current for the same power (P=VI), which reduces power lost to heating in cables (P=I²R)
This makes the National Grid system an efficient way to transfer energy over long distances

nodes.label: Energy transfers in domestic appliances
nodes.objective: Describe how appliances transfer energy from batteries/mains to kinetic energy (motors) or heating
essentialPoints: Domestic appliances are designed to bring about energy transfers
Appliances transfer energy from batteries or ac mains to the kinetic energy store of motors or to heating devices

nodes.label: Equation: energy transferred = power × time (E=Pt)
nodes.objective: Recall and apply E = Pt
essentialPoints: energy transferred (J) = power (W) × time (s)
E = Pt

nodes.label: Function and potential of live, neutral and earth wires
nodes.objective: Describe the function and typical potential of the live, neutral and earth wires
essentialPoints: The live wire carries the alternating pd from the supply, at about 230 V relative to earth
The neutral wire completes the circuit and is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V)
The earth wire is a safety wire at 0 V that only carries current if there is a fault

nodes.label: Interpreting heating and cooling graphs including changes of state
nodes.objective: Interpret temperature-time graphs that show temperature rising, plateauing during a change of state, and rising again.
essentialPoints: Sloped sections show temperature change (energy raising particle kinetic energy)
Flat sections show a change of state occurring at constant temperature (energy raising potential energy)

nodes.label: Calculating specific latent heat of fusion of water from experimental data
nodes.objective: Use measured energy supplied and mass of ice melted to calculate the specific latent heat of fusion of water.
essentialPoints: Rearrange E = mL to find L = E/m
Substitute measured electrical energy and mass melted
specRefs: AT5, latent heat of fusion practical

nodes.label: Count-rate
nodes.objective: Define count-rate as the number of decays recorded per second by a detector.
essentialPoints: Count-rate = number of decays recorded each second by a detector (e.g. Geiger-Muller tube)

nodes.label: Nuclear symbol for an alpha particle
nodes.objective: Represent an alpha particle using standard nuclear notation (mass number 4, atomic number 2, symbol α or He).
essentialPoints: Alpha particle written with mass number 4 and atomic (proton) number 2

nodes.label: Alpha radiation: penetration, range and ionising power
nodes.objective: Describe the penetrating power, range in air and ionising power of alpha radiation.
essentialPoints: Alpha: low penetration (stopped by paper/skin), short range in air, strongly ionising

nodes.label: Nuclear symbol for a beta particle
nodes.objective: Represent a beta particle using standard nuclear notation (mass number 0, charge -1, symbol β).
essentialPoints: Beta particle written with mass number 0 and charge -1

nodes.label: Beta radiation: penetration, range and ionising power
nodes.objective: Describe the penetrating power, range in air and ionising power of beta radiation.
essentialPoints: Beta: medium penetration (stopped by ~few mm aluminium), medium range, moderately ionising

nodes.label: Penetration, range and ionising power of alpha, beta, gamma
nodes.objective: Compare the penetrating power, range in air, and ionising power of alpha, beta, and gamma radiation.
essentialPoints: Alpha: low penetration (stopped by paper/skin), short range in air, strongly ionising
Beta: medium penetration (stopped by ~few mm aluminium), medium range, moderately ionising
Gamma: highly penetrating (needs thick lead/concrete), long range, weakly ionising

nodes.label: Gamma emission causes no change in mass or charge
nodes.objective: State that emission of a gamma ray does not change the mass or charge of the nucleus.
essentialPoints: Gamma emission does not change mass number or atomic number of the nucleus

nodes.label: Gamma radiation: penetration, range and ionising power
nodes.objective: Describe the penetrating power, range in air and ionising power of gamma radiation.
essentialPoints: Gamma: highly penetrating (needs thick lead/concrete), long range, weakly ionising

nodes.label: Neutron absorption triggers induced fission
nodes.objective: Explain that spontaneous fission is rare, and fission is usually triggered by absorption of a neutron by the unstable nucleus.
essentialPoints: Spontaneous fission is rare
Fission is usually initiated when the unstable nucleus first absorbs a neutron

nodes.label: Radiation dose measured in sieverts
nodes.objective: State that radiation dose is measured in sieverts, with 1000 mSv = 1 Sv.
essentialPoints: Radiation dose measured in sieverts (Sv)
1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv)

nodes.label: Braking converts kinetic energy via work done by friction, heating brakes
nodes.objective: Explain that work done by friction between brakes and wheel reduces kinetic energy and raises brake temperature.
essentialPoints: Work done by the friction force between brakes and wheel reduces the vehicle's kinetic energy
This energy transfer raises the temperature of the brakes

nodes.label: Interpreting force-extension data from an investigation
nodes.objective: Interpret data from an investigation of the relationship between force and extension, including identifying the limit of proportionality.
essentialPoints: Identify the linear region and the point where the graph deviates from a straight line
Determine the spring constant from the gradient of the linear region

nodes.label: Work done on a spring equals elastic potential energy stored
nodes.objective: Understand that provided the spring is not inelastically deformed, work done stretching/compressing it equals the elastic potential energy stored.
essentialPoints: Work done on the spring transfers energy entirely into elastic potential energy store
Only true while deformation remains elastic (not inelastic)

nodes.label: Drawing and interpreting velocity-time graphs for terminal velocity
nodes.objective: Draw and interpret velocity-time graphs for objects reaching terminal velocity, relating the shape to the changing forces acting.
essentialPoints: The graph curves as acceleration decreases, flattening to a horizontal line at terminal velocity
Interpret changing gradient in terms of the changing resultant force acting on the object

nodes.label: Investigating air resistance on a falling object (e.g. model parachute)
nodes.objective: Carry out an investigation to measure the effect of air resistance on a falling object such as a model parachute.
essentialPoints: Vary a parameter (e.g. parachute area) and measure falling time/speed
Use timing apparatus to record how air resistance affects motion

nodes.label: RP9 procedure: investigating reflection of light and refraction of light (Physics only)
nodes.objective: Carry out an investigation of reflection of light from different surfaces and refraction of light through different substances using a ray box and protractor.
essentialPoints: Use ray box to direct a light ray onto a surface or through a block, marking ray paths with a pencil
Measure angles of incidence, reflection and refraction with a protractor relative to the normal
Repeat for different surfaces (smooth vs rough) and different substances (e.g. glass, water)

nodes.label: Convex lens: principal focus and focal length
nodes.objective: Describe how a convex lens refracts parallel rays to a principal focus and define focal length.
essentialPoints: A convex lens refracts light, bringing parallel rays to a focus at the principal focus
Focal length is the distance from the lens to the principal focus

nodes.label: Constant temperature means absorption rate equals emission rate (HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain that a body at constant temperature absorbs radiation at the same rate it emits it, and that temperature rises when absorption exceeds emission.
essentialPoints: At constant temperature, a body absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits it
A body's temperature increases when it absorbs radiation faster than it emits it

nodes.label: Application: the generator effect in a given context (HT only)
nodes.objective: Apply the principles of the generator effect to explain behaviour in unfamiliar contexts.
essentialPoints: Use knowledge of induced pd/current, its size factors and direction factors, to explain or predict outcomes in new scenarios

nodes.label: Alternator: generating ac using the generator effect (HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain how the generator effect is used in an alternator to generate alternating current.
essentialPoints: A rotating coil in a magnetic field (or rotating magnet) continuously reverses the direction of induced current as it turns
This produces alternating current (ac)

nodes.label: Dynamo: generating dc using the generator effect (HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain how the generator effect is used in a dynamo to generate direct current.
essentialPoints: A dynamo uses a split-ring commutator to keep the current flowing in one direction
This produces direct current (dc), though its magnitude varies

nodes.label: How a transformer induces current via alternating current (HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain how an alternating current in the primary coil induces a current in the secondary coil.
essentialPoints: Alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic field in the iron core
This changing magnetic field induces an alternating potential difference/current in the secondary coil (via the generator effect)

nodes.label: Equation: F = BIl (HT only)
nodes.objective: Apply the equation force = magnetic flux density × current × length.
essentialPoints: F = B × I × l
force in newtons, N; magnetic flux density in tesla, T; current in amperes, A; length in metres, m
Given on the physics equation sheet

nodes.label: Loudspeakers and headphones (physics only, HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain how a moving-coil loudspeaker and headphones use the motor effect.
essentialPoints: Variations in current in the coil, within a magnetic field, produce a varying force on the coil
This causes the coil and attached cone to vibrate, creating pressure variations (sound waves) that match the variations in current

nodes.label: Interpreting data: patterns, trends, predictions and conclusions
nodes.objective: Interpret data in various forms to identify patterns/trends, make predictions and draw conclusions.
essentialPoints: Patterns and trends in data can be recognised across tabular, graphical and other forms
Conclusions must be drawn directly from, and be limited to, the evidence available

nodes.label: Using the tangent to a curve to find rate of change
nodes.objective: Draw a tangent to a point on a curve and use its slope to determine an instantaneous rate of change.
essentialPoints: A tangent is a straight line touching a curve at one point without crossing it
The gradient of the tangent equals the instantaneous rate of change at that point

nodes.label: Repeatability and reproducibility of measurements
nodes.objective: Distinguish repeatable results (same method/investigator) from reproducible results (different method/investigator).
essentialPoints: Measurements are repeatable if the same investigator repeats the method under the same conditions and gets similar results
Measurements are reproducible if different investigators or different equipment give similar results

nodes.label: RP4: constructing circuits to investigate I-V characteristics
nodes.objective: Use circuit diagrams to construct circuits to investigate I-V characteristics of a filament lamp, diode and resistor at constant temperature
essentialPoints: Construct circuits using circuit diagrams for a filament lamp, diode, and resistor
Vary and reverse the pd across the component and record corresponding current using ammeter and voltmeter
Keep resistor at constant temperature throughout

nodes.label: Application of thermistors in circuits (e.g. thermostat)
nodes.objective: Explain the use of a thermistor in a circuit such as a thermostat
essentialPoints: Thermistors are used in circuits such as thermostats to respond to temperature changes

nodes.label: Application of LDRs in circuits (e.g. switching lights on in the dark)
nodes.objective: Explain the use of an LDR in a circuit such as automatic lighting
essentialPoints: LDRs are used in circuits to switch lights on when it gets dark

nodes.label: Explaining why series resistance increases when adding resistors
nodes.objective: Explain qualitatively why adding resistors in series increases total resistance
essentialPoints: Adding resistors in series increases total resistance because charge must overcome each resistance in turn

nodes.label: Calculating current, pd and resistance in dc series circuits
nodes.objective: Calculate currents, potential differences and resistances in dc series circuits, including equivalent resistance problems
essentialPoints: Combine V=IR with series rules (same current, shared pd, summed resistance) to solve for unknown quantities
Solve problems using the concept of equivalent resistance for resistors in series

nodes.label: Parallel circuits: total resistance less than smallest individual resistance
nodes.objective: State that combined resistance in parallel is less than the smallest individual resistance
essentialPoints: The total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor

nodes.label: Design and use of dc series circuits for measurement/testing
nodes.objective: Explain the design and use of dc series circuits for measurement and testing purposes
essentialPoints: DC series circuits can be designed for specific measurement or testing purposes, using known behaviour of series components

nodes.label: Power ratings and changes in stored energy during appliance use
nodes.objective: Describe the relationship between power ratings of domestic appliances and changes in stored energy when in use
essentialPoints: Higher power-rated appliances transfer energy (and change energy stores) at a faster rate for the same time of use
Examples relate power rating to practical changes in energy stores (e.g. kettle heating water, motor's kinetic store)

nodes.label: Live wire danger even with switch open
nodes.objective: Explain that a live wire may be dangerous even when a switch in the mains circuit is open
essentialPoints: A switch may be placed in the neutral side of a circuit, leaving the live wire still at 230 V even when 'off'
Touching the live wire can therefore still be dangerous with the switch open

nodes.label: Danger of connecting live wire to earth
nodes.objective: Explain the dangers of providing any connection between the live wire and earth
essentialPoints: A connection between live and earth causes a large current to flow suddenly (e.g. through a person or object), which is dangerous
This can cause electric shock or fire

nodes.label: Half-life: definition
nodes.objective: Define half-life in terms of number of nuclei or count-rate/activity falling to half its initial value.
essentialPoints: Half-life = time for the number of nuclei of an isotope in a sample to halve
Equivalently, time for count-rate/activity from the sample to fall to half its initial level

nodes.label: Alpha decay changes mass number and atomic number
nodes.objective: Explain that alpha emission decreases both the mass number (by 4) and atomic number (by 2) of the nucleus.
essentialPoints: Alpha decay decreases mass number by 4
Alpha decay decreases atomic number (charge) by 2

nodes.label: Beta decay changes atomic number but not mass number
nodes.objective: Explain that beta emission does not change mass number but increases atomic number by 1.
essentialPoints: Beta decay does not change the mass number
Beta decay increases the atomic number (charge) by 1

nodes.label: Irradiation
nodes.objective: Define irradiation as exposing an object to nuclear radiation, without the object becoming radioactive.
essentialPoints: Irradiation = process of exposing an object to nuclear radiation
The irradiated object does not itself become radioactive

nodes.label: Evaluating best radiation source for a given situation
nodes.objective: Apply knowledge of penetration, range and ionising power to evaluate the best type of radioactive source for a given use.
essentialPoints: Choice of source depends on required penetration/ionising power for the application
Must weigh benefits (e.g. penetration for imaging) against hazards (e.g. high ionising power near living tissue)

nodes.label: Fission products: two smaller nuclei, neutrons, gamma rays, energy
nodes.objective: Describe the products of a fission event: two smaller nuclei of roughly equal size, two or three neutrons, gamma rays, and released energy.
essentialPoints: Nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei of roughly equal size
Two or three neutrons plus gamma rays are emitted
Energy is released by the fission reaction
All fission products have kinetic energy

nodes.label: Greater speed requires greater braking force for a given stopping distance
nodes.objective: Explain that greater vehicle speed requires greater braking force to stop within a certain distance, and greater braking force gives greater deceleration.
essentialPoints: Higher speed requires greater braking force to stop in the same distance
Greater braking force produces greater deceleration

nodes.label: Calculating stored energy and energy transfers for springs
nodes.objective: Calculate relevant values of elastic potential energy stored and associated energy transfers using experimental or given data.
essentialPoints: Apply Ee = ½ke² using measured/given extension and spring constant values
Relate stored energy to work done during stretching

nodes.label: Convex and concave lens images: real vs virtual
nodes.objective: State that a convex lens can produce either a real or virtual image, whereas a concave lens always produces a virtual image.
essentialPoints: Convex lens images can be real or virtual depending on object distance
Concave lens images are always virtual

nodes.label: Factors determining the temperature of the Earth (HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain how the Earth's temperature depends on the balance of absorption, emission and reflection of radiation.
essentialPoints: Earth's temperature depends on rates of absorption and emission of radiation
It also depends on how much incoming radiation is reflected back into space

nodes.label: Application: drawing/interpreting pd-time graphs for alternators and dynamos (HT only)
nodes.objective: Draw and interpret graphs of potential difference generated in a coil against time for alternators and dynamos.
essentialPoints: Alternator graph is a smooth sinusoidal wave (ac) alternating between positive and negative
Dynamo graph shows pd that stays one sign (all positive or all negative) but varies in magnitude, due to commutator action

nodes.label: Equation: transformer turns ratio (Vp/Vs = np/ns)
nodes.objective: Apply the equation relating primary/secondary potential differences to the number of turns on each coil.
essentialPoints: Vp/Vs = np/ns
Potential differences Vp and Vs measured in volts, V
Given on the physics equation sheet

nodes.label: Relating data to hypotheses in reasoned explanations
nodes.objective: Present reasoned explanations relating data back to a hypothesis, comparing competing hypotheses.
essentialPoints: The extent to which data supports a hypothesis must be explicitly justified using the evidence
Where multiple hypotheses exist, the one better supported by the data should be identified with reasons

nodes.label: Random and systematic error
nodes.objective: Identify potential sources of random and systematic error and explain how each affects results.
essentialPoints: Random error causes results to vary unpredictably and can be reduced by repeating measurements and averaging
Systematic error causes results to differ from the true value by a consistent amount and is not reduced by averaging

nodes.label: Interpreting I-V graphs to identify linear/non-linear behaviour
nodes.objective: Use I-V graphs to distinguish linear and non-linear circuit elements and relate curve shape to component function
essentialPoints: Plot I-V graphs from RP4 data for each component
Identify a straight line through the origin as ohmic (linear) behaviour and a curve as non-ohmic (non-linear)
Relate the curve shape produced to the function/properties of the component (e.g. diode's one-way conduction, lamp's increasing resistance)

nodes.label: Explaining why parallel resistance decreases when adding resistors
nodes.objective: Explain qualitatively why adding resistors in parallel decreases total resistance
essentialPoints: Adding resistors in parallel provides additional paths for charge to flow, decreasing total resistance

nodes.label: Half-life explained through the random nature of decay
nodes.objective: Explain the concept of half-life in terms of the random nature of radioactive decay of individual nuclei.
essentialPoints: Individual nuclear decay is random, but a large sample decays at a predictable average rate
This predictability at large scale gives rise to a consistent, measurable half-life

nodes.label: Determining half-life from given data
nodes.objective: Determine the half-life of a radioactive isotope from given decay data, graphs, or tables.
essentialPoints: Read/interpret decay curve or count-rate table to find time taken for activity to halve

nodes.label: Range of half-life values and effect on hazard
nodes.objective: Explain why hazards from radioactive material differ according to the isotope's half-life.
essentialPoints: Radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values
Short half-life: intensely radioactive for a short time (high initial hazard, decays away quickly)
Long half-life: hazard persists for a very long time even though activity is lower at any moment

nodes.label: Use of nuclear radiation for exploration of internal organs
nodes.objective: Describe how nuclear radiation (tracers) is used to explore internal organs.
essentialPoints: Radioactive tracers are introduced into the body and their emitted radiation (usually gamma) is detected externally to image internal organs

nodes.label: Use of nuclear radiation for control/destruction of unwanted tissue
nodes.objective: Describe how nuclear radiation is used to control or destroy unwanted tissue, e.g. in radiotherapy.
essentialPoints: Radiation (e.g. gamma rays) is targeted at tumours to destroy or control unwanted tissue
Precise dosing/targeting is used to minimise damage to healthy tissue

nodes.label: Balancing nuclear equations for alpha and beta decay
nodes.objective: Use names and symbols of nuclei and particles to write balanced nuclear equations for single alpha or beta decay, balancing mass and atomic numbers.
essentialPoints: Total mass number must balance on both sides of the equation
Total atomic (proton) number must balance on both sides of the equation
Applies to single alpha or beta decay equations (daughter element identification not required)

nodes.label: Comparing hazards of contamination and irradiation
nodes.objective: Compare the hazards associated with contamination versus irradiation, including precautions needed.
essentialPoints: Contamination is an ongoing hazard because the source stays on/in the object
Irradiation hazard exists only while exposed and the object does not remain a source
Suitable precautions (e.g. shielding, distance, time, protective clothing) must be taken during irradiation processes

nodes.label: Chain reaction
nodes.objective: Explain how neutrons released from fission can go on to trigger further fission events, forming a chain reaction.
